chunks.title: Paige O'Hara
chunks.text: Donna Paige Helmintoller, better known as Paige O'Hara (born May 10, 1956), is an American actress, singer and painter.

chunks.title: Paige O'Hara
chunks.text: O'Hara began her career as a Broadway actress in 1983 when she portrayed Ellie May Chipley in the musical "Showboat".

chunks.title: Paige O'Hara
chunks.text: In 1991, she made her motion picture debut in Disney's "Beauty and the Beast", in which she voiced the film's heroine, Belle.

chunks.title: Paige O'Hara
chunks.text: Following the critical and commercial success of "Beauty and the Beast", O'Hara reprised her role as Belle in the film's two direct-to-video follow-ups, "" and "Belle's Magical World".

chunks.title: Something There
chunks.text: "Something There" is a song written by lyricist Howard Ashman and composer Alan Menken for Walt Disney Pictures 30th animated feature film "Beauty and the Beast" (1991).

chunks.title: Something There
chunks.text: Sung by the majority of the film's main cast, the song was recorded by American actors Paige O'Hara as Belle and Robby Benson as the Beast via voice over, featuring actors Jerry Orbach, Angela Lansbury and David Ogden Stiers as Lumiere, Mrs. Potts and Cogsworth, respectively.

chunks.title: Something There
chunks.text: The only song performed by the Beast, "Something There" is heard midway through "Beauty and the Beast "during a scene in which Belle and the Beast finally begin to acknowledge their own feelings for each other.

chunks.title: List of Plymouth Argyle F.C. seasons
chunks.text: Plymouth Argyle Football Club is an English association football club based in Plymouth, Devon.

chunks.title: List of Plymouth Argyle F.C. seasons
chunks.text: They compete in Football League Two, the fourth tier of the English football league system, as of the 2012–13 season.

chunks.title: List of Plymouth Argyle F.C. seasons
chunks.text: The club was founded in 1886 as "Argyle Football Club".

chunks.title: List of Plymouth Argyle F.C. seasons
chunks.text: At this time, there was no League football, so matches were arranged on an ad hoc basis, supplemented by cup competitions.

chunks.title: List of Plymouth Argyle F.C. seasons
chunks.text: In January 1903, the club became a limited company and changed their name to "Plymouth Argyle F.C." Election to the Southern League followed in March, as the club gained direct entry to the First Division for the 1903–04 season.

chunks.title: List of Plymouth Argyle F.C. seasons
chunks.text: The club were also invited to compete in the Western League, a competition which was considered secondary to the Southern League.

chunks.title: 1946–47 Colchester United F.C. season
chunks.text: The 1946–47 season was Colchester United's fifth season in their history and their fifth in the Southern League.

chunks.title: 1946–47 Colchester United F.C. season
chunks.text: Alongside competing in the Southern League, the club also participated in the FA Cup and Southern League Cup.

chunks.title: 1946–47 Colchester United F.C. season
chunks.text: New manager Ted Fenton began to assemble a team of professionals following the reliance on guest players during the 1945–46 season, as the club finished 8th in the league.

chunks.title: 1946–47 Colchester United F.C. season
chunks.text: They reached the first round of the FA Cup, but were defeated by Football League side Reading.

chunks.title: 1946–47 Colchester United F.C. season
chunks.text: They were also Southern League Cup semi-finalists, defeated at Priestfield Stadium by Gillingham.

chunks.title: Bishop's Stortford F.C.
chunks.text: Bishop's Stortford Football Club is a football club based in Bishop's Stortford, Hertfordshire, England.

chunks.title: Bishop's Stortford F.C.
chunks.text: They are currently members of the Southern League Premier Division and play at Woodside Park.

chunks.title: Dover Athletic F.C.
chunks.text: Dover Athletic Football Club is an association football club based in the town of Dover, Kent, England.

chunks.title: Dover Athletic F.C.
chunks.text: The club currently competes in the National League, the fifth tier of English football.

chunks.title: Dover Athletic F.C.
chunks.text: The club was formed in 1983 after the dissolution of the town's previous club, Dover F.C., whose place in the Southern League was taken by the new club.

chunks.title: Dover Athletic F.C.
chunks.text: In the 1989–90 season Dover Athletic won the Southern League championship, but failed to gain promotion to the Football Conference as the club's ground did not meet the required standard.

chunks.title: Dover Athletic F.C.
chunks.text: Three seasons later the team won the title again and this time gained promotion to the Conference, where they spent nine seasons before being relegated at the end of the 2001–02 season.

chunks.title: Dover Athletic F.C.
chunks.text: The club was transferred from the Southern League to the Isthmian League in 2004, competing in that league's Premier Division for one season before mounting financial problems led the club to a further relegation.

chunks.title: Dover Athletic F.C.
chunks.text: In the 2007–08 season, Dover won Division One South of the league, before winning the Premier Division in 2008–09 and thus gaining promotion to the Conference South.

chunks.title: Dover Athletic F.C.
chunks.text: They spent five seasons in this division, reaching the play-offs three times, before defeating Ebbsfleet United in the 2013–14 play-off final to finally return to the Conference Premier after a twelve-year absence.

chunks.title: 1914–15 Watford F.C. season
chunks.text: Watford Football Club are an association football team from the county of Hertfordshire, England.

chunks.title: 1914–15 Watford F.C. season
chunks.text: The 1914–15 season was their nineteenth season of league football, since joining the Southern League as West Hertfordshire for the 1896–97 season.

chunks.title: 1914–15 Watford F.C. season
chunks.text: Watford finished the season as champions of the Southern League First Division, winning 22 and drawing 8 of their 38 league matches.

chunks.title: 1914–15 Watford F.C. season
chunks.text: In other competitions, Watford were eliminated from the FA Cup in the sixth qualifying round by Rochdale, and from the Southern Charity Cup by fellow Southern League team Luton Town.

chunks.title: 1914–15 Watford F.C. season
chunks.text: The club's manager was Harry Kent, and its top scorer George Edmonds, with 17 goals from 35 appearances.

chunks.title: 1914–15 Watford F.C. season
chunks.text: Other notable players included Skilly Williams, who began what would be a 13-year period as the club's first choice goalkeeper, and Fred Gregory, whose goal against Gillingham sealed the title for Watford.

chunks.title: 1914–15 Watford F.C. season
chunks.text: Gregory and Williams were also the only two men to play in all 40 of Watford's games.

chunks.title: List of Millwall F.C. seasons
chunks.text: This is a list of all seasons played by Millwall Football Club from their early beginnings in the Southern League, to their inaugural season in 1920–21 in the English Football League and up to their last completed season.

chunks.title: List of Millwall F.C. seasons
chunks.text: It details their record in the FA Cup, the League Cup and other major competitions entered, as well as managers, top goalscorers and average home attendance for each season.

chunks.title: List of Millwall F.C. seasons
chunks.text: Millwall were founded in 1885 and for the first nine years of their existence did not compete in league football.

chunks.title: List of Millwall F.C. seasons
chunks.text: They first entered the FA Cup in 1887, turning full-time professional as a club in 1890.

chunks.title: List of Millwall F.C. seasons
chunks.text: They were founding members of the Southern League in 1894, which they competed in for 22 seasons, claiming the title twice.

chunks.title: List of Millwall F.C. seasons
chunks.text: They left to join the Football League in 1920.

chunks.title: List of Millwall F.C. seasons
chunks.text: Millwall have played in all four divisions during their 91 seasons in the league, including the Third Division South, which they won twice, in 1928 and 1938.

chunks.title: List of Millwall F.C. seasons
chunks.text: Millwall were Fourth Division champions in 1962.

chunks.title: Kevin Watson
chunks.text: Kevin Edward Watson (born 3 January 1974) is a former professional footballer, turned coach and sports broadcaster.

chunks.title: Kevin Watson
chunks.text: He is currently the manager of Bishop's Stortford.

chunks.title: Poole Town F.C.
chunks.text: Poole Town Football Club is a football club based in Poole, Dorset, England.

chunks.title: Poole Town F.C.
chunks.text: They currently compete in the National League South, the sixth tier of English football, after being promoted as champions of the Southern League Premier Division in the 2015–16 season.

chunks.title: Poole Town F.C.
chunks.text: They were established in 1880 and joined the Western League Division Two in 1930.

chunks.title: Poole Town F.C.
chunks.text: The club is affiliated to the Dorset County Football Association and is a FA Charter Standard Community Club.

chunks.title: Poole Town F.C.
chunks.text: They won the Western League title in 1957 and reached the First Round Proper of the FA Cup four times in their history and the Third Round once, losing to Everton at Goodison.

chunks.title: Poole Town F.C.
chunks.text: They play at the Black Gold Stadium, at Tatnam, Poole, and finished the 2008–09 season as "Double" winners – champions and Dorset Senior Cup winners.

chunks.title: Poole Town F.C.
chunks.text: In 2009–10 they became back-to-back champions of the Wessex League and completed an unprecedented treble winning the League for the 3rd time in a row in 2010–11.

chunks.title: Poole Town F.C.
chunks.text: Promotion to the Southern League was finally achieved after an upgrade to the Tatnam facilities.

chunks.title: Poole Town F.C.
chunks.text: Poole were second in their first season, losing to Gosport in a playoff final and then Champions and promoted to the Southern League Premier Division the following season.

chunks.title: Poole Town F.C.
chunks.text: In 2015-2016 they were promoted to the National League South after finishing as champions of the Southern League.

chunks.title: Poole Town F.C.
chunks.text: In the 2016/17 season there were on course to finish in the playoffs after a prolonged stay in the top 7 places.

chunks.title: Poole Town F.C.
chunks.text: After it was announced they could not participate in the playoff games due to not meeting ground grading requirements by 21st March they suffered a dip in form.

chunks.title: Poole Town F.C.
chunks.text: A late resurgence ensured they finished 5th and had to relinquish the playoff place they had subsequently earned.

chunks.title: 1919–20 Watford F.C. season
chunks.text: Watford Football Club is a association football team from the county of Hertfordshire, England.

chunks.title: 1919–20 Watford F.C. season
chunks.text: The 1919–20 season was their twentieth season of league football, and their first since 1914–15 due to the outbreak of the First World War.

chunks.title: 1919–20 Watford F.C. season
chunks.text: It was also their final season in the Southern League, having originally joined it as West Hertfordshire for the 1896–97 season, prior to a merging with another club and renaming in 1898.

chunks.title: 1919–20 Watford F.C. season
chunks.text: Having started the season as reigning champions, Watford finished the season as runners up of the Southern League First Division on goal average.

chunks.title: 1919–20 Watford F.C. season
chunks.text: They won 26 and drew 6 of their 42 league matches, compared to eventual champions Portsmouth's record of 23 wins and 12 draws.

chunks.title: 1919–20 Watford F.C. season
chunks.text: Watford's only other competitive fixture was in the FA Cup, where they were eliminated in the 6th Qualifying round by fellow Southern League side Southend United.

chunks.title: 1919–20 Watford F.C. season
chunks.text: The club's manager was Harry Kent, and its top scorer was George Edmonds, with 19 goals from 37 appearances.

chunks.title: 1896–97 Southampton St. Mary's F.C. season
chunks.text: The 1896–97 season was the twelfth since the foundation of Southampton St. Mary's F.C. and their third in league football, as members of the Southern League.

chunks.title: 1896–97 Southampton St. Mary's F.C. season
chunks.text: The season was the most successful yet, with St. Mary's claiming the Southern League title for the first time and reaching the Second Round Proper of the FA Cup.

chunks.title: 1896–97 Southampton St. Mary's F.C. season
chunks.text: It was the start of the most successful period in the club's history — in a period of eight years, they were Southern League champions six times and reached the final of the FA Cup twice.

chunks.title: Grigoraș Dinicu
chunks.text: Grigoraș Ionică Dinicu (] ; April 3, 1889 – March 28, 1949) was a Romanian violin virtuoso and composer.

chunks.title: Grigoraș Dinicu
chunks.text: He is most famous for his often-played virtuoso violin showpiece "Hora staccato" (1906) and for making popular the tune Ciocârlia, composed by his grandfather Angheluș Dinicu for "nai" (the Romanian pan flute).

chunks.title: Grigoraș Dinicu
chunks.text: It is rumored that Jascha Heifetz once said that Grigoraș Dinicu was the greatest violinist he had ever heard.

chunks.title: Grigoraș Dinicu
chunks.text: In the 1930s he was involved in the political movement of the Romanian Roma and was made honorary president of the "General Union of the Romanian Roma".

chunks.title: Grigoraș Dinicu
chunks.text: Other well known compositions are: "Hora mărțișorului" ("Mărțișor", literally "little March", is a major Romanian seasonal holiday on March 1st), "Ceasornicul" ("The Clock") and "Căruța poștei" ("The Post Wagon").

chunks.title: Regina Strinasacchi
chunks.text: Regina Schlick née Strinasacchi (c. 1761 - June 11, 1839) was a violin virtuoso and guitarist in a time when women rarely performed on the violin in public.

chunks.title: Regina Strinasacchi
chunks.text: She knew Wolfgang Amadeus Mozart well enough that he composed the Sonata in B flat for Violin and Keyboard, "Strinasacchi," (K. 454) at her request.

chunks.title: Jean-Baptiste Senaillé
chunks.text: Jean Baptiste Senaillé (23 November 1687 in Paris – 15 October 1730 idem) was a French born Baroque composer and violin virtuoso.

chunks.title: Jean-Baptiste Senaillé
chunks.text: His father was a member of Les Vingt-quatre Violons du Roi.

chunks.title: Jean-Baptiste Senaillé
chunks.text: Senaillé studied under Jean-Baptiste Anet, Giovanni Antonio Piani and in Italy under Tomaso Antonio Vitali and imported Italian musical techniques and pieces into the French court.

chunks.title: Jean-Baptiste Senaillé
chunks.text: He wrote around 50 violin sonatas.

chunks.title: Jean-Baptiste Senaillé
chunks.text: He is most well known for a fast 2/4 movement from one of these sonatas, "Allegro Spiritoso", which has had versions published transcribed for a wide variety of instruments, from violoncello to bassoon to euphonium.

chunks.title: Caprice No. 5 (Paganini)
chunks.text: Caprice No. 5 is one of 24 pieces composed by virtuoso violinist Niccolò Paganini in the early 19th century.

chunks.title: Caprice No. 5 (Paganini)
chunks.text: The piece is known for its incredible speed and extremely high technical difficulty.

chunks.title: Caprice No. 5 (Paganini)
chunks.text: Paganini is said to have been able to play it on one string, but there is no evidence to support or refute this.

chunks.title: Alessandro Rolla
chunks.text: Alessandro Rolla (] ; 22 April 175715 September 1841) was an Italian viola and violin virtuoso, composer, conductor and teacher.

chunks.title: Alessandro Rolla
chunks.text: His son, Antonio Rolla, was also a violin virtuoso and composer.

chunks.title: Niccolò Paganini
chunks.text: Niccolò (or Nicolò) Paganini (] ; 27 October 178227 May 1840) was an Italian violinist, violist, guitarist, and composer.

chunks.title: Niccolò Paganini
chunks.text: He was the most celebrated violin virtuoso of his time, and left his mark as one of the pillars of modern violin technique.

chunks.title: Niccolò Paganini
chunks.text: His 24 Caprices for Solo Violin Op. 1 are among the best known of his compositions, and have served as an inspiration for many prominent composers.

chunks.title: Tzigane
chunks.text: Tzigane is a rhapsodic composition by the French composer Maurice Ravel.

chunks.title: Tzigane
chunks.text: It was commissioned by and dedicated to Hungarian violinist Jelly d'Arányi, great-niece of the influential violin virtuoso Joseph Joachim.

chunks.title: Tzigane
chunks.text: The original instrumentation was for violin and piano (with optional luthéal attachment).

chunks.title: Tzigane
chunks.text: The first performance took place in London on April 26, 1924 with the dedicatee on violin and with Henri Gil-Marchex at the piano (with luthéal).

chunks.title: Franz Pecháček
chunks.text: Franz Xaver Pecháček (4 July 1793 in Vienna – 15 September 1840 in Karlsruhe) was an Austrian-German violin virtuoso and composer of Bohemian origin.

chunks.title: Franz Pecháček
chunks.text: Besides polonaises, variations, Rondos and potpourris for violin and orchestra, he composed two string quartets and the "Adagio et Polonaise" for clarinet and orchestra.

chunks.title: Schnuckenack Reinhardt
chunks.text: Franz "Schnuckenack" Reinhardt (17 February 1921 – 15 April 2006) was a gypsy jazz musician (violinist), composer and interpreter.

chunks.title: Schnuckenack Reinhardt
chunks.text: He was considered the "great violin virtuoso of Sinti music."

chunks.title: Schnuckenack Reinhardt
chunks.text: He was a German Sinto; his music was mostly published and categorized under the contemporary names gypsy jazz or "Musik deutscher Zigeuner" (music of German gypsies).

chunks.title: Schnuckenack Reinhardt
chunks.text: He "made this music accessible to a broad public" and made the most significant contribution to the presentation of gypsy music and jazz in Germany into a concert form.

chunks.title: Schnuckenack Reinhardt
chunks.text: He was the pioneer of this style of music in Germany and directly or indirectly inspired many of the succeeding generation of gypsy jazz players in that country, as well as preserving on record a great many folkloric and gypsy compositions for future generations.

chunks.title: Michael Christian Festing
chunks.text: Michael Christian Festing (29 November 1705 – 24 July 1752) was an English violinist and composer.

chunks.title: Michael Christian Festing
chunks.text: His reputation lies mostly on his work as a violin virtuoso.

chunks.title: Bus Stop (TV series)
chunks.text: Bus Stop is a 26-episode American drama which aired on ABC from October 1, 1961, until March 25, 1962, starring Marilyn Maxwell as Grace Sherwood, the owner of a bus station and diner in the fictitious town of Sunrise in the Colorado Rockies.

chunks.title: Bus Stop (TV series)
chunks.text: The program was adapted from William Inge's play, "Bus Stop", and Inge was a script consultant for the series, which followed the lives of travelers passing through the bus station and the diner.

chunks.title: Bus Stop (TV series)
chunks.text: Maxwell's co-stars were Richard Anderson as District Attorney Glenn Wagner, Rhodes Reason as Sheriff Will Mayberry, Joan Freeman as waitress Elma Gahrigner, Bernard Kates as Ralph the coroner, and Buddy Ebsen as Virge Blessing.

chunks.title: The Mickey Rooney Show
chunks.text: The Mickey Rooney Show (also known as Hey, Mulligan) is an American sitcom that aired from 1954 to 1955 on NBC.

chunks.title: The Mickey Rooney Show
chunks.text: The series stars Mickey Rooney (in his first television role) who was particularly remembered for his starring role in numerous Andy Hardy films made between 1937 and 1958, which overlapped with "Hey Mulligan".

chunks.title: Bob Hope
chunks.text: Bob Hope, KBE, KC*SG, KSS (born Leslie Towns Hope; May 29, 1903 – July 27, 2003) was an American comedian, vaudevillian, actor, singer, dancer, athlete and author.

chunks.title: Bob Hope
chunks.text: With a career spanning nearly 80 years, Hope appeared in more than 70 short and feature films, including a series of "Road" movies.

chunks.title: Bob Hope
chunks.text: In addition to hosting the Academy Awards show nineteen times, more than any other host, he appeared in many stage productions and television roles, and was the author of 14 books.

chunks.title: Bob Hope
chunks.text: The song "Thanks for the Memory" is widely regarded as his signature tune.

chunks.title: A Miser Brothers' Christmas
chunks.text: A Miser Brothers' Christmas is a stop motion spin-off special based on some of the characters from the 1974 Rankin-Bass special "The Year Without a Santa Claus".

chunks.title: A Miser Brothers' Christmas
chunks.text: Distributed by Warner Bros.

chunks.title: A Miser Brothers' Christmas
chunks.text: Animation under their Warner Premiere label (the rights holders of the post-1974 Rankin-Bass library) and Toronto-based Cuppa Coffee Studios, the one-hour special premiered on ABC Family on Saturday, December 13, 2008, during the network's annual The 25 Days of Christmas programming.

chunks.title: A Miser Brothers' Christmas
chunks.text: Mickey Rooney and George S. Irving reprised their respective roles as Santa Claus and Heat Miser at ages 88 and 86.

chunks.title: A Miser Brothers' Christmas
chunks.text: Snow Miser, originally portrayed by Dick Shawn who died in 1987, was voiced by Juan Chioran, while Mrs. Claus, voiced by Shirley Booth in the original, was portrayed by Catherine Disher (because Booth had died in 1992).

chunks.title: A Miser Brothers' Christmas
chunks.text: The movie aimed to emulate the Rankin/Bass animation style.

chunks.title: A Miser Brothers' Christmas
chunks.text: This is the last Christmas special to feature Mickey Rooney as Santa Claus, as he died in 2014, as well as the last time George Irving voiced Heat Miser, as he died in 2016.

chunks.title: The Atomic Kid
chunks.text: The Atomic Kid is a 1954 American black-and-white science fiction comedy film from Republic Pictures, produced by Maurice Duke and Mickey Rooney, directed by Leslie H. Martinson, that stars Mickey Rooney and Robert Strauss.

chunks.title: Mickey's Helping Hand
chunks.text: Mickey's Medicine Man is a 1931 talkie short film in Larry Darmour's "Mickey McGuire" series starring a young Mickey Rooney.

chunks.title: Mickey's Helping Hand
chunks.text: Directed by Jesse Duffy, the two-reel short was released to theaters on December 19, 1931 by RKO Radio Pictures.

chunks.title: Mickey's Helping Hand
chunks.text: It was one of the few Mickey McGuire shorts without Mickey Rooney in the cast.

chunks.title: Off Limits (1953 film)
chunks.text: Off Limits is a 1953 comedy film directed by George Marshall and starring Bob Hope, Mickey Rooney and Marilyn Maxwell.

chunks.title: Off Limits (1953 film)
chunks.text: Hope plays a manager who enlists in the army to keep an eye on his boxer, who has been drafted.

chunks.title: Off Limits (1953 film)
chunks.text: The picture was written by Hal Kanter and Jack Sher, and was released in the UK as Military Policemen, as the characters played by Hope and Rooney join the military police.

chunks.title: The Extraordinary Seaman
chunks.text: The Extraordinary Seaman is a 1969 American comedy war film directed by John Frankenheimer and starring David Niven, Faye Dunaway, Alan Alda, Mickey Rooney, and Jack Carter.

chunks.title: The Extraordinary Seaman
chunks.text: Apart from his participation in the documentaries "That's Entertainment!

chunks.title: The Extraordinary Seaman
chunks.text: " (1974), and "That's Entertainment!

chunks.title: The Extraordinary Seaman
chunks.text: III" (1994), the movie is notable for being the last film Mickey Rooney acted in which was released by Metro-Goldwyn-Mayer.

chunks.title: Mickey Rooney Jr.
chunks.text: Mickey Rooney Jr. (born Joseph Yule III; July 3, 1945) is an American former actor, and the eldest son of the actor Mickey Rooney.

chunks.title: Mickey Rooney Jr.
chunks.text: He operates the Rooney Entertainment Group, a movie and TV production company.

chunks.title: Mickey Rooney Jr.
chunks.text: He is a born-again Christian, and he has an evangelical ministry in Hemet, California.

chunks.title: The Adventures of the Black Stallion
chunks.text: The Adventures of The Black Stallion is a television series that starred Mickey Rooney and Richard Ian Cox, as a trainer and a teenaged horse racer and was loosely based on the book series by Walter Farley.

chunks.title: The Adventures of the Black Stallion
chunks.text: The series originally ran on The Family Channel and YTV from September 15, 1990 to May 16, 1993, before cancellation.

chunks.title: The Adventures of the Black Stallion
chunks.text: It has since been shown in re-runs throughout the world.

chunks.title: The Adventures of the Black Stallion
chunks.text: Mickey Rooney is the only original cast member from "The Black Stallion" to reprise his role in the show.

chunks.title: Liebeslieder Polkas
chunks.text: Liebeslieder Polkas is recording of the music of Peter Schickele under his comic pseudonym of P. D. Q. Bach.

chunks.title: Liebeslieder Polkas
chunks.text: It describes itself as "the first opus of P.D.Q. Bach to be discovered in which he inflicted his music on the work of well-known poets, or even known poets, for that matter" and includes "the ambitious zodiac song cycle, the "Twelve Quite Heavenly Songs"."

chunks.title: Liebeslieder Polkas
chunks.text: The album was released on Vanguard Records in 1980, with a cover image of Schickele mimicking a famous image of Johannes Brahms at the piano.

chunks.title: Brahms' Lullaby
chunks.text: Cradle Song is the common name for a number of children's lullabies with similar lyrics, the original of which was Johannes Brahms' "Wiegenlied: Guten Abend, gute Nacht " ("Good evening, good night"), Op.

chunks.title: Brahms' Lullaby
chunks.text: 49, No. 4, published in 1868 and widely known as Brahms' Lullaby.

chunks.title: Brahms' Lullaby
chunks.text: The lyrics of the first verse are from a collection of German folk poems called "Des Knaben Wunderhorn" and the second stanza was written by (1824–1909) in 1849.

chunks.title: Brahms' Lullaby
chunks.text: The lullaby's melody is one of the most famous and recognizable in the world, used by countless parents to sing their babies to sleep.

chunks.title: Brahms' Lullaby
chunks.text: The Lullaby was dedicated to Brahms' friend, Bertha Faber, on the occasion of the birth of her second son.

chunks.title: Brahms' Lullaby
chunks.text: Brahms had been in love with her in her youth and constructed the melody of the "Wiegenlied " to suggest, as a hidden counter-melody, a song she used to sing to him.

chunks.title: Brahms' Lullaby
chunks.text: The lullaby was first performed in public on 22 December 1869 in Vienna by Louise Dustmann (singer) and Clara Schumann (piano).

chunks.title: Sixteen Waltzes, Op. 39 (Brahms)
chunks.text: Sixteen Waltzes, Op.

chunks.title: Sixteen Waltzes, Op. 39 (Brahms)
chunks.text: 39 is a set of 16 short waltzes for piano written by Johannes Brahms.

chunks.title: Sixteen Waltzes, Op. 39 (Brahms)
chunks.text: They were composed in 1865, and published two years later, dedicated to the music critic Eduard Hanslick.

chunks.title: Piano Sonata No. 3 (Brahms)
chunks.text: The Piano Sonata No. 3 in F minor, Op. 5 of Johannes Brahms was written in 1853 and published the following year.

chunks.title: Piano Sonata No. 3 (Brahms)
chunks.text: The sonata is unusually large, consisting of five movements, as opposed to the traditional three or four.

chunks.title: Piano Sonata No. 3 (Brahms)
chunks.text: When he wrote this piano sonata, the genre was seen by many to be past its heyday.

chunks.title: Piano Sonata No. 3 (Brahms)
chunks.text: Brahms, enamored of Beethoven and the classical style, composed Piano Sonata No. 3 with a masterful combination of free Romantic spirit and strict classical architecture.

chunks.title: Piano Sonata No. 3 (Brahms)
chunks.text: As a further testament to Brahms' affinity for Beethoven, the Piano Sonata is infused with the instantly recognizable motive from Beethoven's Symphony No. 5 during the first, third, and fourth movements.

chunks.title: Piano Sonata No. 3 (Brahms)
chunks.text: Composed in Düsseldorf, it marks the end of his cycle of three sonatas, and was presented to Robert Schumann in November of that year; it was the last work that Brahms submitted to Schumann for commentary.

chunks.title: Piano Sonata No. 3 (Brahms)
chunks.text: Brahms was barely 20 years old at its composition.

chunks.title: Piano Sonata No. 3 (Brahms)
chunks.text: The piece is dedicated to Countess Ida von Hohenthal of Leipzig.

chunks.title: Bruce Tammen
chunks.text: Bruce Tammen is a conductor and artistic director.

chunks.title: Bruce Tammen
chunks.text: Tammen holds degrees from Luther College, Northwestern University, and the University of Chicago and has taught voice and directed choirs at Luther College, the University of Chicago, and the University of Virginia.

chunks.title: Bruce Tammen
chunks.text: Tammen studied extensively in France with Dalton Baldwin and Gerard Souzay, and for several years studied with Max van Egmond at Oberlin's Baroque Performance Institute.

chunks.title: Bruce Tammen
chunks.text: He has performed several seasons under Helmuth Rilling at the Oregon Bach Festival, and with the Robert Shaw Choral Institute, in Souillac, France.

chunks.title: Bruce Tammen
chunks.text: Tammen is baritone soloist on the Telarc/Shaw compact discs Appear and Inspire and Liebeslieder Waltzes.

chunks.title: Bruce Tammen
chunks.text: The Chicago Chorale, conducted by Tammen, received the top performance of the year by the Chicago Classical Review with a performance of Rodion Shchedrin's "The Sealed Angel.

chunks.title: Bruce Tammen
chunks.text: Bruce Tammen is married to Esther Menn.

chunks.title: Bruce Tammen
chunks.text: They have three sons; Joseph, Elijah, and Daniel Tammen, as well as a daughter Kaia Tammen.

chunks.title: Neue Liebeslieder
chunks.text: Neue Liebeslieder (New love songs), Op.

chunks.title: Neue Liebeslieder
chunks.text: 65, written by Johannes Brahms, is a collection of Romantic pieces written for four solo voices and four hands on the piano.

chunks.title: Neue Liebeslieder
chunks.text: They are also known as "Neue Liebesliederwalzer".

chunks.title: Neue Liebeslieder
chunks.text: "Neue Liebeslieder" were written during the Romantic period between 1869 and 1874.

chunks.title: Neue Liebeslieder
chunks.text: The text of the songs is adapted from folk songs of various areas of Europe including Turkey, Poland, Latvia and Sicily.

chunks.title: Neue Liebeslieder
chunks.text: The text for songs 1 through 14 were translated and compiled by Georg Friedrich Daumer in his poem series, "Polydora"; the text for the fifteenth and final song, entitled "Zum Schluß" (In Conclusion), was written by Johann Wolfgang von Goethe.

chunks.title: Ländler
chunks.text: The Ländler (] ) is a folk dance in  time which was popular in Austria, south Germany, German Switzerland, and Slovenia at the end of the 18th century.

chunks.title: Liebeslieder Walzer, Op. 52 (Brahms)
chunks.text: Johannes Brahms' Liebeslieder Waltzes ("Liebeslieder-Walzer") are distributed across two opus numbers: Op. 52 and Op.

chunks.title: Liebeslieder Walzer, Op. 52 (Brahms)
chunks.text: The waltzes are a collection of love songs in Ländler style for voices and piano four hands.

chunks.title: Liebeslieder Walzer, Op. 52 (Brahms)
chunks.text: The lyrics for the "Liebeslieder" come from Georg Friedrich Daumer's "Polydora", a collection of folk songs and love poems.

chunks.title: Liebeslieder Walzer, Op. 52 (Brahms)
chunks.text: While there is no concrete record indicating the exact inspiration for the Waltzes, there is speculation that Brahms' motivation for the songs was his frustrated love for pianist Clara Schumann, composer Robert Schumann's wife.

chunks.title: Clarinet Sonatas (Brahms)
chunks.text: The Clarinet Sonatas, Op. 120, Nos. 1 and 2 are a pair of works written for clarinet and piano by the Romantic composer Johannes Brahms.

chunks.title: Clarinet Sonatas (Brahms)
chunks.text: They were written in 1894 and are dedicated to the clarinetist Richard Mühlfeld.

chunks.title: Clarinet Sonatas (Brahms)
chunks.text: The sonatas stem from a period late in Brahms’s life where he “discovered” the beauty of the sound and tonal colour of the clarinet.

chunks.title: Clarinet Sonatas (Brahms)
chunks.text: The form of the clarinet sonata was largely undeveloped until after the completion of these sonatas, after which the combination of clarinet and piano was more readily used in composers’ new works.

chunks.title: Clarinet Sonatas (Brahms)
chunks.text: These were the last chamber pieces Brahms wrote before his death and are considered two of the great masterpieces in the clarinet repertoire.

chunks.title: Clarinet Sonatas (Brahms)
chunks.text: Brahms also produced a frequently performed transcription of these works for viola with alterations to better suit the instrument.

chunks.title: Johannes Brahms Medal
chunks.text: The Johannes Brahms Medal (German: Johannes-Brahms-Medaille) of Hamburg is a music award established in 1928, named after the composer Johannes Brahms who was born in Hamburg.

chunks.title: Meadowbrook State Parkway
chunks.text: The Meadowbrook State Parkway (also known as the Meadowbrook, the Meadowbrook Parkway or the MSP) is a 12.52 mi parkway in Nassau County, New York, in the United States.

chunks.title: Meadowbrook State Parkway
chunks.text: Its southern terminus is at a full cloverleaf interchange with the Bay and Ocean parkways in Jones Beach State Park.

chunks.title: Meadowbrook State Parkway
chunks.text: The parkway heads north, crossing South Oyster Bay and intersecting Loop Parkway before crossing onto the mainland and connecting to the Southern State Parkway in North Merrick.

chunks.title: Meadowbrook State Parkway
chunks.text: It continues north to the village of Carle Place, where the Meadowbrook Parkway ends at exit 31A of the Northern State Parkway.

chunks.title: Meadowbrook State Parkway
chunks.text: The Meadowbrook Parkway is designated New York State Route 908E (NY 908E), an unsigned reference route.

chunks.title: Meadowbrook State Parkway
chunks.text: Most of the road is limited to non-commercial traffic, like most parkways in the state of New York; however, the portion south of Merrick Road is open to commercial traffic.

chunks.title: Sunken Meadow State Parkway
chunks.text: The Sunken Meadow State Parkway (also known as the Sunken Meadow) is a 6.19 mi long parkway in Suffolk County, Long Island, New York.

chunks.title: Sunken Meadow State Parkway
chunks.text: Located entirely within the town of Smithtown, the parkway begins at a cloverleaf interchange with the Northern State Parkway (exits 44–45) and the northern terminus of the Sagtikos State Parkway.

chunks.title: Sunken Meadow State Parkway
chunks.text: The parkway, which continues north, is a northern spur of the Sagtikos, which opened in September 1952.

chunks.title: Sunken Meadow State Parkway
chunks.text: The northern end of the parkway is at the toll barrier in exit SM5 in the Kings Park section of Smithtown.

chunks.title: Sunken Meadow State Parkway
chunks.text: From there, the road continues north through Sunken Meadow State Park to a roundabout at the Long Island Sound.

chunks.title: Sunken Meadow State Parkway
chunks.text: The parkway comprises the northern half of New York State Route 908K (NY 908K, an unsigned reference route), with the Sagtikos State Parkway forming the southern portion.

chunks.title: Sunken Meadow State Parkway
chunks.text: Commercial vehicles are, like on most parkways, prohibited from using the Sunken Meadow, except for a portion north of NY 25A in Kings Park.

chunks.title: Sagtikos State Parkway
chunks.text: The Sagtikos State Parkway, also known as the Sagtikos or Sagtikos Parkway, known colloquially as "the Sag" is a 5.14 mi north–south limited-access parkway in Suffolk County on Long Island, New York, in the United States.

chunks.title: Sagtikos State Parkway
chunks.text: It begins at an interchange with the Southern and Heckscher state parkways in the hamlet of West Islip and goes north to a large cloverleaf interchange with the Northern State Parkway in the town of Smithtown, where the Sagtikos ends and the road becomes the Sunken Meadow State Parkway.

chunks.title: Sagtikos State Parkway
chunks.text: The parkway comprises the southern half of New York State Route 908K (NY 908K), an unsigned reference route, with the Sunken Meadow State Parkway forming the northern portion.

chunks.title: Sagtikos State Parkway
chunks.text: Commercial vehicles are prohibited from using the Sagtikos State Parkway, a restriction that applies to most parkways in the state.

chunks.title: Southern State Parkway
chunks.text: The Southern State Parkway (also known as the Southern State or Southern Parkway) is a 25.53 mi limited-access highway on Long Island, New York, in the United States.

chunks.title: Southern State Parkway
chunks.text: The parkway begins at an interchange with the Belt and Cross Island parkways in Elmont, in Nassau County, and travels east to an interchange with the Sagtikos State Parkway in West Islip, Suffolk County, where it becomes the Heckscher State Parkway.

chunks.title: Southern State Parkway
chunks.text: The Southern State Parkway comprises the western portion of unsigned New York State Route 908M (NY 908M), with the Heckscher Parkway occupying the eastern section.

chunks.title: Mosholu Parkway
chunks.text: The Mosholu Parkway is a hybrid freeway-standard parkway and grade-level roadway in the New York City borough of the Bronx, constructed from 1935 to 1937 as part of the roadway network created under Robert Moses.

chunks.title: Mosholu Parkway
chunks.text: The roadway extends for 3.0 mi between the New York Botanical Garden (where its southeast end meets the Bronx River Parkway) and Van Cortlandt Park (where its northwest end meets the Henry Hudson Parkway).

chunks.title: Mosholu Parkway
chunks.text: The New York City Department of Transportation is responsible for the operation and maintenance of the roadway while the New York City Department of Parks and Recreation is responsible for the surrounding rights-of-way.

chunks.title: Mosholu Parkway
chunks.text: The parkway is designated as New York State Route 908F (NY 908F), an unsigned reference route, by the New York State Department of Transportation.

chunks.title: Northern State Parkway
chunks.text: The Northern State Parkway (also known as the Northern State or Northern Parkway) is a 28.88 mi limited-access state parkway on Long Island in the U.S. state of New York.

chunks.title: Northern State Parkway
chunks.text: The western terminus is at the Queens–Nassau County line, where the parkway continues westward into New York City as the Grand Central Parkway.

chunks.title: Northern State Parkway
chunks.text: The eastern terminus is at New York State Route 347 (NY 347) and NY 454 in Hauppauge.

chunks.title: Northern State Parkway
chunks.text: The parkway is designated New York State Route 908G (NY 908G), an unsigned reference route.

chunks.title: Northern State Parkway
chunks.text: As its name implies, the parkway services communities along the northern half of the island.

chunks.title: Robert Moses
chunks.text: Robert Moses (December 18, 1888 – July 29, 1981) was a public official who worked mainly in the New York metropolitan area.

chunks.title: Robert Moses
chunks.text: Known as the "master builder" of mid-20th century New York City, Long Island, Rockland County, and Westchester County, he is sometimes compared to Baron Haussmann of Second Empire Paris, and was one of the most polarizing figures in the history of urban development in the United States.

chunks.title: Robert Moses
chunks.text: His decisions favoring highways over public transit helped create the modern suburbs of Long Island and influenced a generation of engineers, architects, and urban planners who spread his philosophies across the nation despite not training in those professions.

chunks.title: Robert Moses
chunks.text: Moses would call himself a "coordinator" and was referred to in the media as a "master builder".

chunks.title: Merritt Parkway
chunks.text: The Merritt Parkway (also known locally as "The Merritt") is a historic limited-access parkway in Fairfield County, Connecticut, the first of its kind.

chunks.title: Merritt Parkway
chunks.text: Designed for Connecticut's Gold Coast, the parkway is known for its scenic layout, its uniquely styled signage, and the architecturally elaborate overpasses along the route.

chunks.title: Merritt Parkway
chunks.text: It is designated as a National Scenic Byway and is also listed in the National Register of Historic Places.

chunks.title: Merritt Parkway
chunks.text: Signed as part of Route 15, it runs from the New York state line in Greenwich, where it serves as the continuation of the Hutchinson River Parkway, to the Housatonic River in Stratford, where the Wilbur Cross Parkway begins.

chunks.title: Merritt Parkway
chunks.text: Facing bitter opposition, the project took six years to build in three different sections, with the Connecticut Department of Transportation constantly requiring additional funding due to the area's high property value.

chunks.title: Merritt Parkway
chunks.text: The parkway was named for U.S. Congressman Schuyler Merritt.

chunks.title: Merritt Parkway
chunks.text: On May 19, 2010, the Merritt Parkway was named one of America's Most Endangered Historic Places.

chunks.title: Pelham Parkway
chunks.text: The Bronx and Pelham Parkway (usually referred to simply as Pelham Parkway) is a 2.25-mile (3.62 km) long parkway in the borough of the Bronx in New York City.

chunks.title: Pelham Parkway
chunks.text: Despite the parkway moniker, Pelham Parkway is a local street, with two main roadways (one in each direction), and two service roads.

chunks.title: Pelham Parkway
chunks.text: Like other parkways in New York City, commercial traffic is disallowed, and is redirected to the service roads.

chunks.title: Pelham Parkway
chunks.text: Pelham Parkway runs from the Bronx River Parkway (at a mutual junction with U.S. Route 1 or US 1 within Bronx Park) out to Pelham Bay Park, hence the name, as it connects the two parks.

chunks.title: Pelham Parkway
chunks.text: A bikeway runs alongside.

chunks.title: Pelham Parkway
chunks.text: At the eastern end, it intersects with Interstate 95 (I-95, named the New England Thruway at this point).

chunks.title: Pelham Parkway
chunks.text: Though the parkway ends here, the road itself continues as Shore Road.

chunks.title: Pelham Parkway
chunks.text: At its west end, it continues as East Fordham Road, then West Fordham Road (after passing Jerome Avenue) and in Manhattan as West 207th Street.

chunks.title: Pelham Parkway
chunks.text: The residential neighborhood that surrounds the parkway is known by the same name.

chunks.title: Heckscher State Parkway
chunks.text: The Heckscher State Parkway (formerly known as the Heckscher Spur) is an 8.24 mi parkway on Long Island, New York, in the United States.

chunks.title: Heckscher State Parkway
chunks.text: The parkway, located entirely within the Suffolk County town of Islip, begins at the south end of the Sagtikos State Parkway in West Islip, from where it continues west as the Southern State Parkway.

chunks.title: Heckscher State Parkway
chunks.text: It proceeds east as a six-lane parkway through Brentwood and Central Islip, loosely paralleling New York State Route 27 (NY 27).

chunks.title: Heckscher State Parkway
chunks.text: At Islip Terrace, the Heckscher Parkway turns southward, crossing NY 27 before ending at the toll barrier for Heckscher State Park in Great River.

chunks.title: Heckscher State Parkway
chunks.text: The parkway comprises the eastern portion of New York State Route 908M (NY 908M), an unsigned reference route, with the Southern State Parkway occupying the western section.

chunks.title: Heckscher State Parkway
chunks.text: In order to avoid confusion, the highway is signed as an extension of the Southern State Parkway west of the NY 27 interchange (exit 44).

chunks.title: Southeastern Conference
chunks.text: The Southeastern Conference (SEC) is an American college athletic conference whose member institutions are located primarily in the Southern part of the United States.

chunks.title: Southeastern Conference
chunks.text: Its fourteen members include the flagship public universities of ten states, three additional public land grant universities, and one private research university.

chunks.title: Southeastern Conference
chunks.text: The conference is headquartered in Birmingham, Alabama.

chunks.title: Southeastern Conference
chunks.text: The SEC participates in the National Collegiate Athletic Association (NCAA) Division I in sports competitions; for football, it is part of the Football Bowl Subdivision (FBS), formerly known as Division I-A.

chunks.title: 1899 Tennessee Volunteers football team
chunks.text: The 1899 Tennessee Volunteers football team represented the University of Tennessee in the 1899 Southern Intercollegiate Athletic Association football season.

chunks.title: 1899 Tennessee Volunteers football team
chunks.text: They were the first UT team to have a head coach.

chunks.title: 1899 Tennessee Volunteers football team
chunks.text: J. A. Pierce helmed the team in 1899 and 1900.

chunks.title: 1899 Tennessee Volunteers football team
chunks.text: The 1899 Tennessee Volunteers won six games and lost two.

chunks.title: 1984 Tennessee Volunteers football team
chunks.text: The 1984 Tennessee Volunteers football team (variously "Tennessee", "UT" or the "Vols") represented the University of Tennessee in the 1984 NCAA Division I-A football season.

chunks.title: 1984 Tennessee Volunteers football team
chunks.text: Playing as a member of the Southeastern Conference (SEC), the team was led by head coach Johnny Majors, in his eighth year, and played their home games at Neyland Stadium in Knoxville, Tennessee.

chunks.title: 1984 Tennessee Volunteers football team
chunks.text: They finished the season with a record of seven wins, four losses and one tie (7–4–1 overall, 3–3 in the SEC) and a loss against Maryland in the Sun Bowl.

chunks.title: 1984 Tennessee Volunteers football team
chunks.text: The Volunteers offense scored 327 points while the defense allowed 276 points.

chunks.title: 1983 Tennessee Volunteers football team
chunks.text: The 1983 Tennessee Volunteers Tennessee Volunteers football team (variously "Tennessee", "UT" or the "Vols") represented the University of Tennessee in the 1983 NCAA Division I-A football season.

chunks.title: 1983 Tennessee Volunteers football team
chunks.text: Playing as a member of the Southeastern Conference (SEC), the team was led by head coach Johnny Majors, in his seventh year, and played their home games at Neyland Stadium in Knoxville, Tennessee.

chunks.title: 1983 Tennessee Volunteers football team
chunks.text: They finished the season with a record of nine wins and three losses (9–3 overall, 4–2 in the SEC) and a victory over Maryland in the Florida Citrus Bowl.

chunks.title: 1983 Tennessee Volunteers football team
chunks.text: The Volunteers offense scored 282 points while the defense allowed 165 points.

chunks.title: 1985 Tennessee Volunteers football team
chunks.text: The 1985 Tennessee Volunteers football team (variously "Tennessee", "UT" or the "Vols") represented the University of Tennessee in the 1985 NCAA Division I-A football season.

chunks.title: 1985 Tennessee Volunteers football team
chunks.text: Playing as a member of the Southeastern Conference (SEC), the team was led by head coach Johnny Majors, in his ninth year, and played their home games at Neyland Stadium in Knoxville, Tennessee.

chunks.title: 1985 Tennessee Volunteers football team
chunks.text: They finished the season with a record of nine wins, one loss and two ties (9–1–2 overall, 5–1 in the SEC), as SEC champions and with a victory over Miami in the 1986 Sugar Bowl.

chunks.title: 1985 Tennessee Volunteers football team
chunks.text: The Volunteers offense scored 325 points while the defense allowed 140 points.

chunks.title: 1985 Tennessee Volunteers football team
chunks.text: At season’s end, the Volunteers ranked fourth in both the AP Poll and the Coaches' Poll.

chunks.title: Tennessee Volunteers football statistical leaders
chunks.text: The Tennessee Volunteers football statistical leaders are individual statistical leaders of the Tennessee Volunteers football program in various categories, including passing, rushing, receiving, total offense, defensive stats, and kicking.

chunks.title: Tennessee Volunteers football statistical leaders
chunks.text: Within those areas, the lists identify single-game, single-season, and career leaders.

chunks.title: Tennessee Volunteers football statistical leaders
chunks.text: The Volunteers represent University of Tennessee in the NCAA's Southeastern Conference.

chunks.title: 1891 Tennessee Volunteers football team
chunks.text: The 1891 Tennessee Volunteers football team represented the University of Tennessee in the 1891 season.

chunks.title: 1891 Tennessee Volunteers football team
chunks.text: This was the first Tennessee Volunteers football team.

chunks.title: 1891 Tennessee Volunteers football team
chunks.text: They traveled on Thanksgiving Day to Chattanooga, Tennessee to face Sewanee.

chunks.title: 1891 Tennessee Volunteers football team
chunks.text: They had no head coach and were mainly an intramural team.

chunks.title: 1896 Tennessee Volunteers football team
chunks.text: The 1896 Tennessee Volunteers football team represented the University of Tennessee in the 1896 college football season.

chunks.title: 1896 Tennessee Volunteers football team
chunks.text: It was the first official Tennessee Volunteers football team since 1893.

chunks.title: 1896 Tennessee Volunteers football team
chunks.text: The 1896 Vols went undefeated at 4–0 for the first winning season in school history.

chunks.title: 1896 Tennessee Volunteers football team
chunks.text: This was also the Tennessee's first season in the Southern Intercollegiate Athletic Association (SIAA), though they did not play a conference opponent.

chunks.title: 1938 Tennessee Volunteers football team
chunks.text: The 1938 Tennessee Volunteers football team represented the University of Tennessee in the 1938 season.

chunks.title: 1938 Tennessee Volunteers football team
chunks.text: Head coach Robert Neyland fielded his third team at Tennessee after returning from active duty in the United States Army.

chunks.title: 1938 Tennessee Volunteers football team
chunks.text: The 1938 Tennessee Volunteers won the school's first national championship and are regarded as one of the greatest teams in SEC and NCAA history.

chunks.title: 1930 Tennessee Volunteers football team
chunks.text: The 1930 Tennessee Volunteers football team (variously "Tennessee", "UT" or the "Vols") represented the University of Tennessee in the 1930 college football season.

chunks.title: 1930 Tennessee Volunteers football team
chunks.text: Playing as a member of the Southern Conference (SoCon), the team was led by head coach Robert Neyland, in his fifth year, and played their home games at Shields-Watkins Field in Knoxville, Tennessee.

chunks.title: 1930 Tennessee Volunteers football team
chunks.text: The 1930 Vols won nine and lost one game (9–1 overall, 6–1 in the SoCon).

chunks.title: 1930 Tennessee Volunteers football team
chunks.text: The only loss of the season came on October 18 to eventual Rose Bowl champion, Alabama.

chunks.title: 1930 Tennessee Volunteers football team
chunks.text: Tennessee and Vanderbilt were the only teams to score against Alabama in 1930.

chunks.title: 1930 Tennessee Volunteers football team
chunks.text: The 1930 Volunteers team outscored their opponents 209 to 31 and posted seven shutouts

chunks.title: KWCH-DT
chunks.text: KWCH-DT, virtual channel 12 (UHF digital channel 19), is a CBS-affiliated television station serving Wichita, Kansas, United States that is licensed to Hutchinson.

chunks.title: KWCH-DT
chunks.text: The station is owned by Gray Television, as part of a duopoly with CW affiliate KSCW-DT (channel 33); Gray also operates Univision affiliate KDCU-DT (channel 31) under a joint sales agreement with owner Entravision Communications Corporation.

chunks.title: KWCH-DT
chunks.text: KWCH and KSCW share studio facilities and KDCU's master control operations are located on 37th Street in northeast Wichita; KWCH maintains transmitter facilities located in rural northeastern Reno County (south-southeast of Buhler).

chunks.title: KSCW-DT
chunks.text: KSCW-DT, virtual channel 33 (VHF digital channel 12), is a CW-affiliated television station licensed to Wichita, Kansas, United States.

chunks.title: KSCW-DT
chunks.text: The station is owned by Gray Television, as part of a duopoly with CBS affiliate KWCH-DT (channel 12); Gray also operates Univision affiliate KDCU-DT (channel 31) under a joint sales agreement with owner Entravision Communications Corporation.

chunks.title: KSCW-DT
chunks.text: KSCW and KWCH share studio facilities and KDCU's master control operations are located on East 37th Street North in northeastern Wichita; KSCW maintains transmitter facilities located in rural northeastern Reno County (due south of Buhler).

chunks.title: KDCU-DT
chunks.text: KDCU-DT, virtual and UHF digital channel 31, is a Univision-affiliated television station serving Wichita, Kansas, United States that is licensed to Derby.

chunks.title: KDCU-DT
chunks.text: The station is owned by the Entravision Communications Corporation; Gray Television, which owns CBS affiliate KWCH-DT (channel 12) and CW affiliate KSCW-DT (channel 33), operates KDCU under a joint sales agreement.

chunks.title: KDCU-DT
chunks.text: KDCU's offices and master control operations are based at KWCH and KSCW's joint studio facilities on 37th Street in northeast Wichita; KDCU maintains transmitter facilities located in rural northwestern Sedgwick County (northeast of Colwich).

chunks.title: KDCU-DT
chunks.text: On cable, the station is available in standard definition on Cox Communications channel 15 and AT&T U-verse channel 31, and in high definition on Cox digital channel 2015 and U-verse channel 1031.

chunks.title: KHSL-TV
chunks.text: KHSL-TV, virtual channel 12 (UHF digital channel 43) is a CBS-affiliated television station located in Chico, California, United States, that also serves Redding.

chunks.title: KHSL-TV
chunks.text: The station is owned by Heartland Media as part of a duopoly with NBC affiliate KNVN (channel 24), which is owned by Maxair Media but operated by Heartland through a local marketing agreement.

chunks.title: KHSL-TV
chunks.text: The two stations share studios at the corner of Eaton Road and Silverbell Road on the northwest side of Chico, while its transmitter is located along Cohasset Road in rural Butte County northwest of Paradise.

chunks.title: KXMB-TV
chunks.text: KXMB-TV, channel 12, is the CBS-affiliated television station for Bismarck, North Dakota.

chunks.title: KXMB-TV
chunks.text: It broadcasts a high definition digital signal on VHF channel 12 (or virtual channel 12.1 via PSIP) from a transmitter near St. Anthony.

chunks.title: KXMB-TV
chunks.text: The station can also be seen on Midcontinent cable channel 11 in Bismarck-Mandan, and cable channel 12 in most other areas.

chunks.title: KXMB-TV
chunks.text: There is a high definition feed provided on Midcontinent digital channel 611.

chunks.title: WDJT-TV
chunks.text: WDJT-TV, virtual channel 58 (UHF digital channel 46), is a CBS-affiliated television station licensed to Milwaukee, Wisconsin, United States.

chunks.title: WDJT-TV
chunks.text: The station is owned by Chicago-based Weigel Broadcasting, as part of a duopoly with Racine-licensed independent station WMLW-TV (channel 49), and is also a sister station to MeTV owned-and-operated station WBME-CD (channel 41, which is also carried via WDJT's DT2 subchannel) and Telemundo affiliate WYTU-LD (channel 63).

chunks.title: WDJT-TV
chunks.text: All four stations share studio facilities located on South 60th Street in Milwaukee (near West Allis); WDJT's transmitter is located in Milwaukee's Lincoln Park (next to the transmitter belonging to ABC affiliate WISN-TV, channel 12).

chunks.title: WFLD
chunks.text: WFLD, virtual channel 32 (UHF digital channel 31), is a Fox owned-and-operated television station licensed to Chicago, Illinois, United States.

chunks.title: WFLD
chunks.text: The station is owned by the Fox Television Stations division of 21st Century Fox, and operates as part of a television duopoly with Gary, Indiana-licensed primary CW affiliate and secondary MyNetworkTV owned-and-operated station WPWR-TV (channel 50).

chunks.title: WFLD
chunks.text: The two stations share studio and office facilities located at Michigan Plaza on North Michigan Avenue in the Chicago Loop; WFLD's transmitter is based at the Willis Tower on South Wacker Drive in the Loop business district.

chunks.title: WFLD
chunks.text: On cable, the station can be seen on Comcast Xfinity channel 12 in most parts of the Chicago area.

chunks.title: WTLV
chunks.text: WTLV, virtual channel 12 (VHF digital channel 13), is an NBC-affiliated television station licensed to Jacksonville, Florida, United States.

chunks.title: WTLV
chunks.text: The station is owned by the Tegna Media division of Tegna, Inc., as part of a duopoly with Orange Park-licensed ABC affiliate WJXX (channel 25).

chunks.title: WTLV
chunks.text: The two stations share studio facilities on East Adams Street (near EverBank Field) in downtown Jacksonville; WTLV's transmitter is located on Eve Drive in the city's Killarney Shores section.

chunks.title: WJXX
chunks.text: WJXX, virtual channel 25 (VHF digital channel 10), is an ABC-affiliated television station serving Jacksonville, Florida, United States that is licensed to Orange Park.

chunks.title: WJXX
chunks.text: The station is owned by the Tegna Media division of Tegna, Inc., as part of a duopoly with Jacksonville-licensed NBC affiliate WTLV (channel 12) (ironically a former ABC affiliate itself from 1980 to 1988).

chunks.title: WJXX
chunks.text: The two stations share studio facilities on East Adams Street (near EverBank Field) in downtown Jacksonville; WJXX's transmitter is located on Eve Drive in the city's Kilarney Shores section.

chunks.title: KMBC-TV
chunks.text: KMBC-TV, virtual channel 9 (UHF digital channel 29), is the ABC-affiliated television station licensed to Kansas City, Missouri, United States and also serving Kansas City, Kansas.

chunks.title: KMBC-TV
chunks.text: The station is owned by the Hearst Television subsidiary of the Hearst Corporation, as part of a duopoly with CW affiliate KCWE (channel 29).

chunks.title: KMBC-TV
chunks.text: The two stations share studio facilities located at the Winchester Business Center on Winchester Avenue and East 63rd Street (near Swope Park, off of I-435) in southeastern Kansas City, Missouri; KMBC-TV maintains transmitter facilities located near the Blue River in eastern Kansas City.

chunks.title: Everyday (Ariana Grande song)

chunks.title: Everyday (Ariana Grande song)

chunks.title: Everyday (Ariana Grande song)

chunks.text: "Applause" was inspired by the cheering of her fans, which kept her motivated during the months she toured with the Born This Way Ball in pain, before cancelling it due to a hip injury.

chunks.title: World Faith
chunks.text: World Faith is an international NGO founded in 2008 by Frank Fredericks.

chunks.title: World Faith
chunks.text: The organization’s stated mission is "to end religious violence.”

chunks.title: World Faith
chunks.text: It aims to promote opportunities for interfaith dialogue through community service projects to “[foster] genuine dialogue that is built around the shared values of service” and to “[inspire] project participants to build cross-identity friendships and strengthen their understanding of other religious traditions.”

chunks.title: World Faith
chunks.text: World Faith’s activities pivot around the idea of revising the system of global peacebuilding, with a special focus on the role of faith identity in conflict.

chunks.title: Octobass
chunks.text: The octobass is an extremely large and rare (only 7 in existence) bowed string instrument that was first built around 1850 in Paris by the French luthier Jean-Baptiste Vuillaume (1798–1875).

chunks.title: Octobass
chunks.text: It has three strings and is essentially a larger version of the double bass (the specimen in the collection of the Musée de la Musique in Paris measures in length, whereas a full-size double bass is generally approximately in length).

chunks.title: Octobass
chunks.text: Because of the extreme fingerboard length and string thickness, the musician plays it using a system of levers and pedals.

chunks.title: Octobass
chunks.text: It has never been produced on a large scale or used much by composers (though Hector Berlioz wrote favorably about the instrument and proposed its widespread adoption).

chunks.title: Octobass
chunks.text: In addition to the Paris instrument, octobasses exist in the collections of the Musical Instrument Museum in Phoenix, Arizona and the Kunsthistorisches Museum in Vienna.

chunks.title: Talk Dirty (Jason Derulo song)

chunks.title: Talk Dirty (Jason Derulo song)

chunks.title: Talk Dirty (Jason Derulo song)

chunks.title: Talk Dirty (Jason Derulo song)

chunks.title: Quogue (LIRR station)

chunks.title: Quogue (LIRR station)
chunks.text: During construction the station was moved by the village "on a Sunday morning" from its original and current location to a location on Old Depot Road.

chunks.title: Quogue (LIRR station)
chunks.text: The second depot was built around 1882 and later was moved to a private location around 1905.

chunks.title: Quogue (LIRR station)
chunks.text: The third depot was built around 1905 and at some point was elevated for the bridge over the former New York State Route 113.

chunks.title: Quogue (LIRR station)
chunks.text: The station house was razed around April, 1964 but the station stop itself continued to operate until March 16, 1998.

chunks.title: Quogue (LIRR station)
chunks.text: This station, along with nine others around that time were closed due to low ridership, which did not make it very cost-effective to build high-level platforms to support the new C3 railcars the LIRR was procuring at the time.

chunks.title: Xyloband
chunks.text: Xylobands are wristbands that contain light-emitting diodes and radio frequency receivers.

chunks.title: Xyloband
chunks.text: The lights inside the wristband can be controlled by a software program, which sends signals to the wristband, instructing it to light up or blink, for example.

chunks.title: Xyloband
chunks.text: The RGB version has a white strap and can emit any colour on the spectrum.

chunks.title: Xyloband
chunks.text: The single colour version is available in green, blue, yellow, red, pink and white.

chunks.title: Xyloband
chunks.text: The first use of Xylobands on a large scale was on Coldplay's 2012 Mylo Xyloto tour.

chunks.title: Xyloband
chunks.text: A Xyloband was given to each member of the audience, and as the concert played, the flashing of the bands was synchronized to the music.

chunks.title: Xyloband
chunks.text: The inventor of the wristbands, Jason Regler, stated that he had the idea for the flashing wristbands while at a Coldplay concert, during the song "Fix You".

chunks.title: Ask (The Smiths song)
chunks.text: "Ask" is a song recorded by the English rock band the Smiths.

chunks.title: Ask (The Smiths song)
chunks.text: It was released as a single on 20 October 1986 through Rough Trade Records.

chunks.title: Ask (The Smiths song)
chunks.text: Credited to vocalist Morrissey and guitarist Johnny Marr, "Ask" is an upbeat, positive pop song built around major chords.

chunks.title: Ask (The Smiths song)
chunks.text: Its lyrics touch on shyness and encourages the listener to release their inhibitions.

chunks.title: Ask (The Smiths song)
chunks.text: Its multiple guitar parts and complex production led to disagreements regarding its final mix.

chunks.title: Ask (The Smiths song)
chunks.text: In addition, Craig Gannon, one-time rhythm guitarist for the group, has claimed he wrote and was denied credit for the song's chord structure.

chunks.title: Fix You

chunks.title: Do You... (Miguel song)

chunks.title: Do You... (Miguel song)

chunks.title: Condamine Power Station
chunks.text: Condamine Power Station is a 140 MW combined cycle power station near Miles on the western Darling Downs in Queensland, Australia.

chunks.title: Condamine Power Station
chunks.text: The station is located 8 km east of Miles on the south side of the Warrego Highway.

chunks.title: Condamine Power Station
chunks.text: The Condamine Power Station is owned by QGC Limited, a subsidiary of BG Group.

chunks.title: Condamine Power Station
chunks.text: It has been claimed to be the world’s first combined-cycle power station entirely fired by untreated coal seam gas and Australia's first steam turbine condenser cooled by coal seam methane waste water.

chunks.title: Condamine Power Station
chunks.text: However, the Townsville Power Station at Yabulu, which was converted from a peak load power station to burn only coal seam gas in a combined cycle configuration, was commissioned much earlier, in February 2005.

chunks.title: Korba Thermal Power Station
chunks.text: The Korba Thermal Power Station or Korba East Thermal Power Station is a coal-fired power station at Korba East in Chhattisgarh, India.

chunks.title: Korba Thermal Power Station
chunks.text: The power station is owned and operated by Chhattisgarh State Power Generation Company, publicly owned generation utility formed in 2009 following the restructuring of the Chhattisgarh State Electricity Board.

chunks.title: Reeves Plains Power Station
chunks.text: Reeves Plains Power Station is a proposal from Alinta Energy to build a gas-fired power station at Reeves Plains between Gawler and Mallala in South Australia.

chunks.title: Reeves Plains Power Station
chunks.text: The proposed site borders both the Moomba-Adelaide gas pipe and an electricity transmission line.

chunks.title: Reeves Plains Power Station
chunks.text: The power station is proposed to use six gas turbines to produce up to 300 MW of electricity.

chunks.title: Reeves Plains Power Station
chunks.text: It is expected to be operated at a peaking plant rather than running full time.

chunks.title: Reeves Plains Power Station
chunks.text: The primary source of fuel will be the gas pipeline, however the plant will also be able to operate on diesel fuel, and will have diesel storage on site.

chunks.title: Reeves Plains Power Station
chunks.text: Stage 1 is expected to only be two or three of the turbines, generating 100 to 150 MW of electricity.

chunks.title: Reeves Plains Power Station
chunks.text: The power station is expected to take 12 months to build, and be commissioned in January 2019.

chunks.title: Alinta Energy
chunks.text: Alinta Energy is an Australian generation, electricity and gas retailing private company that is owned by Hong Kong-based Chow Tai Fook Enterprises.

chunks.title: Alinta Energy
chunks.text: Alinta Energy has an owned and contracted generation portfolio of up to 1,957 MW, approximately 800,000 combined electricity and gas retail customers and around 450 employees across Australia and New Zealand.

chunks.title: Tarong North Power Station
chunks.text: Tarong North Power Station is a 443 megawatt coal fired power station on the same site as Tarong Power Station in the South Burnett.

chunks.title: Tarong North Power Station
chunks.text: The Queensland Government commissioned the construction of the power station in November 1999.

chunks.title: Tarong North Power Station
chunks.text: Construction work began in 2000.

chunks.title: Tarong North Power Station
chunks.text: The power station was initially owned by a 50/50 joint venture between Tarong Energy and TM Energy.

chunks.title: Tarong North Power Station
chunks.text: Full ownership of the power station by Tarong Energy was obtained in November 2009.

chunks.title: Jablanica Dam
chunks.text: The Jablanica Dam is an arch-gravity dam on the Neretva River about 4 km northeast of Jablanica in the Herzegovina-Neretva Canton of Bosnia and Herzegovina.

chunks.title: Jablanica Dam
chunks.text: The dam was constructed between 1947 and 1955 with the primary purpose of hydroelectric power production.

chunks.title: Jablanica Dam
chunks.text: The power station was commissioned in two stages, from 1955 until 1958.

chunks.title: Jablanica Dam
chunks.text: The first generator was commissioned in February 1955.

chunks.title: Jablanica Dam
chunks.text: An upgrade in 2008 increased the installed capacity of the power station from 150 MW to 180 MW.

chunks.title: Jablanica Dam
chunks.text: The dam's power station is located about 4.4 km to the southeast near Jablanica and discharges back into the Neretva River.

chunks.title: Jablanica Dam
chunks.text: It contains six 30 MW Francis turbine-generators for an installed capacity of 180 MW.

chunks.title: Jablanica Dam
chunks.text: The difference in elevation between the reservoir and power station afford a hydraulic head (water drop) of 111 m .

chunks.title: Jablanica Dam
chunks.text: The dam is 85 m tall and creates Jablanica lake.

chunks.title: Jablanica Dam
chunks.text: The dam and power station are owned and operated by Elektroprivreda Bosne i Hercegovine.

chunks.title: Tongbai Pumped Storage Power Station
chunks.text: The Tongbai Pumped Storage Power Station is a pumped-storage hydroelectric power station located 6 km north of Tiantai city in Tiantai County of Zhejiang Province, China.

chunks.title: Tongbai Pumped Storage Power Station
chunks.text: Construction on the power station began in May 2000 and the first unit was commissioned in December 2005.

chunks.title: Tongbai Pumped Storage Power Station
chunks.text: The remaining three were operational by December 2006.

chunks.title: Tongbai Pumped Storage Power Station
chunks.text: The entire project cost US$904.10 million, of which US$320 million was provided by the World Bank.

chunks.title: Tongbai Pumped Storage Power Station
chunks.text: The power station operates by shifting water between an upper and lower reservoir to generate electricity.

chunks.title: Tongbai Pumped Storage Power Station
chunks.text: The lower reservoir was formed with the creation of the Tongbai Lower Dam on the Baizhang River.

chunks.title: Tongbai Pumped Storage Power Station
chunks.text: The Tongbai Upper Reservoir, which already existed before construction began, is in an adjacent valley above the east side of the lower reservoir on Tongbai Creek.

chunks.title: Tongbai Pumped Storage Power Station
chunks.text: During periods of low energy demand, such as at night, water is pumped from Tongbai Lower Reservoir up to the upper reservoir.

chunks.title: Tongbai Pumped Storage Power Station
chunks.text: When energy demand is high, the water is released back down to the lower reservoir but the pump turbines that pumped the water up now reverse mode and serve as generators to produce electricity.

chunks.title: Tongbai Pumped Storage Power Station
chunks.text: The process is repeated as necessary and the plant serves as a peaking power plant.

chunks.title: Tongbai Pumped Storage Power Station
chunks.text: The power station is operated by Shenergy Company.

chunks.title: Bełchatów Power Station
chunks.text: The Bełchatów Power Station is the world's second largest (nameplate power of 5,420 MW) lignite-fired power station situated near Bełchatów in Łódź Voivodeship, Poland.

chunks.title: Bełchatów Power Station
chunks.text: It is the largest thermal power station in Europe, and second largest fossil-fuel power station in the world.

chunks.title: Bełchatów Power Station
chunks.text: It produces 27–28 TWh of electricity per year, or 20% of the total power generation in Poland.

chunks.title: Bełchatów Power Station
chunks.text: The power station is owned and operated by PGE GIEK Oddział Elektrownia Bełchatów, a subsidiary of Polska Grupa Energetyczna.

chunks.title: Millmerran Power Station
chunks.text: The Millmerran Power Station is a coal-fired power station south of Millmerran in the Darling Downs region of Queensland, Australia.

chunks.title: Millmerran Power Station
chunks.text: The power station was commissioned in 2002 and cost $1.5 billion to build.

chunks.title: Millmerran Power Station
chunks.text: The power station is owned and operated by InterGen, a multinational company owned by the Ontario Teachers' Pension Plan and AIG Highstar Capital II, a private equity fund sponsored by a subsidiary of American International Group, Inc.

chunks.title: Lake Margaret Power Station
chunks.text: The Lake Margaret Power Stations comprise two hydroelectric power stations located in Western Tasmania, Australia.

chunks.title: Lake Margaret Power Station
chunks.text: The power stations are part of the KingYolande Power Scheme and are owned and operated by Hydro Tasmania.

chunks.title: Lake Margaret Power Station
chunks.text: Officially the Upper Lake Margaret Power Station, a conventional hydroelectric power station, and the Lower Lake Margaret Power Station, a mini-hydroelectric power station, the stations are generally collectively referred to in the singular format as the Lake Margaret Power Station.

chunks.title: Lake Margaret Power Station
chunks.text: The stations are located approximately 2.5 km apart.

chunks.title: 2011 NBA All-Star Game
chunks.text: The 2011 NBA All-Star Game was an exhibition basketball game that was played on February 20, 2011 at Staples Center in Los Angeles, California, home of the Los Angeles Clippers and the Los Angeles Lakers.

chunks.title: 2011 NBA All-Star Game

chunks.title: 2011 NBA All-Star Game
chunks.text: The Clippers and Lakers were both awarded the All-Star Game in an announcement by commissioner David Stern on June 9, 2009.

chunks.title: 2011 NBA All-Star Game
chunks.text: This was the second time that the Staples Center had hosted the All-Star Game; the arena had previously hosted the event in 2004.

chunks.title: 2011 NBA All-Star Game
chunks.text: This will be the fifth time that Los Angeles had hosted the All-Star Game; before Staples Center opened in 1999, the city had previously hosted the event in 1963, 1972, and 1983.

chunks.title: 2011 NBA All-Star Game

chunks.title: Lakers–Clippers rivalry
chunks.text: The Lakers–Clippers rivalry is a National Basketball Association (NBA) rivalry between the Los Angeles Lakers and Los Angeles Clippers.

chunks.title: Lakers–Clippers rivalry
chunks.text: The two Pacific Division teams both play their home games at Staples Center in Los Angeles, inspiring their matchups to sometimes be called the "Hallway Series".

chunks.title: Lakers–Clippers rivalry
chunks.text: The Lakers relocated from Minneapolis in 1960, while the Clippers moved from San Diego in 1984.

chunks.title: Lakers–Clippers rivalry
chunks.text: Los Angeles fans have historically favored the Lakers.

chunks.title: Lakers–Clippers rivalry
chunks.text: But the Clippers have sold out every home game at Staples Center since Feb. 2011 and entered the 2016–17 season with the sixth-longest active sellout streak in the NBA.

chunks.title: Lakers–Clippers rivalry
chunks.text: The Lakers have won 11 of their 16 NBA championships since moving to Los Angeles.

chunks.title: Lakers–Clippers rivalry
chunks.text: Meanwhile, the Clippers have made the playoffs only nine times since 1984 and were long considered the laughingstock of the NBA; in the history of the franchise, they have never advanced past the second round of the playoffs.

chunks.title: Lakers–Clippers rivalry
chunks.text: Some contended that the term "rivalry" was inaccurate until the Clippers became more successful.

chunks.title: Lakers–Clippers rivalry
chunks.text: For the first time in 20 years, the Clippers won the season series against the Lakers in 2012–13.

chunks.title: Lakers–Clippers rivalry
chunks.text: This was the first of five straight season series victories for the Clippers, which included season sweeps in both 2014-15 and 2015-16.

chunks.title: Lakers–Clippers rivalry
chunks.text: With the Clippers' 3-1 series win in 2016-17, the Lakers have now won the season series just four times in the past 13 seasons, with five Clippers wins, four Lakers wins, and four ties.

chunks.title: Lakers–Clippers rivalry
chunks.text: The Lakers hold a 99–47 advantage in the all-time series against the Clippers.

chunks.title: Lakers–Clippers rivalry
chunks.text: The two teams have never met in the playoffs.

chunks.title: Quin Snyder

chunks.title: Martinus Dom

chunks.title: Mariastern Abbey, Banja Luka
chunks.text: Mariastern Abbey () is Trappist abbey in Bosnia and Herzegovina, situated near the country's second largest city Banja Luka.

chunks.title: Mariastern Abbey, Banja Luka
chunks.text: It consists of the Church of the Assumption of the Blessed Virgin Mary and the monastery of Trappist monks.

chunks.title: Mariastern Abbey, Banja Luka

chunks.title: Mariastern Abbey, Banja Luka

chunks.title: Rochefort Abbey
chunks.text: The Trappist Abbey of Rochefort or Abbey of Notre-Dame de Saint-Rémy, which belongs to the Cistercians of Strict Observance, is located in Rochefort in the province of Namur (Wallonia, Belgium).

chunks.title: Rochefort Abbey
chunks.text: The abbey is famous for its spiritual life and its brewery, which is one of few Trappist beer breweries in the world.

chunks.title: Rochefort Abbey
chunks.text: Life in the abbey is characterised by prayer, reading and manual work, the three basic elements of Trappist life.

chunks.title: Rochefort Abbey
chunks.text: The motto of the abbey is "Curvata Resurgo".

chunks.title: Westmalle Brewery
chunks.text: Westmalle Brewery (Brouwerij der Trappisten van Westmalle) is a Trappist brewery in the Westmalle Abbey, Belgium.

chunks.title: Westmalle Brewery

chunks.title: Westmalle Brewery

chunks.title: Achel Abbey
chunks.text: The Trappist Abbey of Achel or Saint Benedictus-Abbey or also Achelse Kluis (which means hermitage of Achel), which belongs to the Cistercians of Strict Observance, is located in Achel in the Campine region of the province of Limburg (Flanders, Belgium).

chunks.title: Achel Abbey

chunks.title: Achel Abbey
chunks.text: Life in the abbey is characterised by prayer, reading and manual work, the three basic elements of Trappist life.

chunks.title: Achel Brewery

chunks.title: Trappist beer

chunks.title: Trappist beer

chunks.title: St. Joseph's Abbey, Massachusetts
chunks.text: St. Joseph's Abbey is a monastery of the Catholic Order of Cistercians of the Strict Observance (O.C.S.O.), popularly known as the "Trappists," located in Spencer, Massachusetts.

chunks.title: St. Joseph's Abbey, Massachusetts

chunks.title: St. Joseph's Abbey, Massachusetts

chunks.title: Hamont-Achel

chunks.title: Sian Gibson
