chunks.title: Georgia (coffee)
chunks.text: As of 2007, in Japan, Georgia's sales double the sales of Coca-Cola.

chunks.title: Georgia (coffee)
chunks.text: Georgia is one of many brands of Japanese canned coffee.

chunks.title: Georgia (coffee)
chunks.text: Georgia coffee was introduced in the United States in 2009, where it is almost exclusively sold in Asian grocery stores.

chunks.title: Naval Air Station Ellyson Field
chunks.text: Naval Air Station Ellyson Field was a former U.S. Navy training base, established in Escambia County, Florida in 1940 at the outset of World War II as an auxiliary facility to Chevalier Field at Naval Air Station Pensacola, Florida.

chunks.title: Naval Air Station Ellyson Field
chunks.text: Originally designated Base Field 01913 (Site 3), located on the west side of Escambia Bay 16 miles northeast of NAS Pensacola, construction on an expanded facility, officially named Ellyson Field in honor of CDR Theodore G. “Spuds” Ellyson, the Navy’s first aviator, began on 26 February 1941.

chunks.title: Naval Air Station Ellyson Field
chunks.text: It had three red brick hangars common to the various Navy airfields in the Pensacola area, and eight paved runways, the longest of which was 3,550 ft in length.

chunks.title: Harvey Point Defense Testing Activity
chunks.text: The Harvey Point Defense Testing Activity facility, owned by the Department of Defense, is located on a peninsula in Perquimans County, North Carolina, along the Albemarle Sound, near the city of Hertford, NC.

chunks.title: Harvey Point Defense Testing Activity
chunks.text: It was established in World War II as Naval Auxiliary Air Station Harvey Point, an operating base for sea planes conducting anti-submarine surveillance off the Atlantic coast.

chunks.title: Harvey Point Defense Testing Activity
chunks.text: A close-by naval facility, Naval Air Station Weeksville, served as a blimp base from 1941 to 1957, while another former naval air facility remains active as Coast Guard Air Station Elizabeth City.

chunks.title: Brewton Municipal Airport
chunks.text: Brewton Municipal Airport (FAA LID: 12J) is a city-owned public-use airport located 3 NM south of the central business district of Brewton, a city in Escambia County, Alabama, United States.

chunks.title: Brewton Municipal Airport
chunks.text: Originally constructed by the U.S. Navy during World War II as an auxiliary field to the Naval Air Station Pensacola complex, it was later redesignated as Navy Outlying Landing Field (NOLF) Brewton before being conveyed to the city of Brewton as a public use facility.

chunks.title: Brewton Municipal Airport
chunks.text: Although under civilian ownership, the airfield still functions concurrently as NOLF Brewton and is used by Navy training aircraft located at Naval Air Station Whiting Field, Florida.

chunks.title: Naval Air Station Glenview
chunks.text: Naval Air Station Glenview or NAS Glenview was an operational U.S. Naval Air Station from 1923 to 1995.

chunks.title: Naval Air Station Glenview
chunks.text: Located in Glenview, Illinois, a suburb of Chicago, the air base primarily operated training aircraft as well as seaplanes on nearby Lake Michigan during World War II.

chunks.title: Naval Air Station Glenview
chunks.text: Reconfigured as a Naval Air Reserve base following World War II, NAS Glenview supported Naval Air Reserve, Marine Air Reserve/4th Marine Aircraft Wing, and U.S. Army Reserve 244th Aviation Group as well as an active duty Coast Guard Air Station.

chunks.title: Carrier Air Wing One
chunks.text: Carrier Air Wing One (CVW-1) is a United States Navy aircraft carrier air wing based at Naval Air Station Oceana, Virginia, with most of its various squadrons also home based at NAS Oceana.

chunks.title: Carrier Air Wing One
chunks.text: Additional squadrons are based at Naval Station Norfolk/Chambers Field, Virginia; Marine Corps Air Station Beaufort, South Carolina; Naval Air Station Whidbey Island, Washington; and Naval Air Station Jacksonville, Florida.

chunks.title: Carrier Air Wing One
chunks.text: Carrier Air Wing One is assigned to USS Harry S. Truman (CVN 75).

chunks.title: Grand Prairie Armed Forces Reserve Complex
chunks.text: The Grand Prairie Armed Forces Reserve Complex (formerly Naval Air Station Dallas or Hensley Field) is a former United States Navy Naval Air Station located on Mountain Creek Lake in southwest Dallas.

chunks.title: Grand Prairie Armed Forces Reserve Complex
chunks.text: The installation was originally established as an Army Aviation center, and eventually became home to aviation assets from all the military services.

chunks.title: Grand Prairie Armed Forces Reserve Complex
chunks.text: The facility was decommissioned as a naval air station in December 1998 pursuant to BRAC action and the extant Naval Air Reserve, Marine Air Reserve and Texas Air National Guard flying units (wings, groups, squadrons) relocating to the nearby former Carswell AFB, which was concurrently transferred to U.S. Navy custody via the Base Realignment and Closure Commission action and renamed Naval Air Station Joint Reserve Base Fort Worth / Carswell Field.

chunks.title: Coast Guard Air Station Corpus Christi
chunks.text: Coast Guard Air Station Corpus Christi is an Air Station of the United States Coast Guard located in Corpus Christi, Texas.

chunks.title: Coast Guard Air Station Corpus Christi
chunks.text: The Station is co-located with Sector Corpus Christi offices at Naval Air Station Corpus Christi.

chunks.title: Coast Guard Air Station Corpus Christi
chunks.text: The Coast Guard Air Detachment was established on 20 November 1950, and served the entire western Gulf of Mexico with one PBY-5 Catalina fixed wing aircraft, and four pilots.

chunks.title: Coast Guard Air Station Corpus Christi
chunks.text: In 1965, the detachment was formally designated USCG Air Station Corpus Christi.

chunks.title: Coast Guard Air Station Corpus Christi
chunks.text: Early aircraft consisted of HU-16E Albatross, HH-52A Seaguard helicopter, HC-131 Samaritan, and HU-25A fanjet's.

chunks.title: Coast Guard Air Station Corpus Christi
chunks.text: Following extensive personnel and equipment changes in the operations department, the air station became fully operational on October 15, 1980, and operated as one of thirteen Coast Guard Group units between Port O'Connor, Texas and the Mexican border.

chunks.title: Coast Guard Air Station Corpus Christi
chunks.text: The Station, maintained a 24-hour Search and rescue capability, with the use of three HH-52A helicopters and three HU-25A fanjet's.

chunks.title: Coast Guard Air Station Corpus Christi
chunks.text: The Unit averaged over 400 rescues a year, which included searches for overdue vessels, assisting sinking or disabled boats, and medical evacuations from offshore oil rigs.

chunks.title: Coast Guard Air Station Corpus Christi
chunks.text: In the spring of 1986 the station's HH-52s were replaced with the Aérospatiale HH-65 Dolphin helicopter.

chunks.title: Coast Guard Air Station Corpus Christi
chunks.text: In May 2005 the Coast Guard commissioned Air station Corpus Christi to combine all the units within the area of Port Lavaca to Brownsville under one unified command.

chunks.title: Naval Air Station Pensacola
chunks.text: Naval Air Station Pensacola or NAS Pensacola (IATA: NPA, ICAO: KNPA, FAA LID: NPA) (formerly NAS/KNAS until changed circa 1970 to allow Nassau International Airport, now Lynden Pindling International Airport, to have IATA code NAS), "The Cradle of Naval Aviation", is a United States Navy base located next to Warrington, Florida, a community southwest of the Pensacola city limits.

chunks.title: Naval Air Station Pensacola
chunks.text: It is best known as the initial primary training base for all U.S.Navy, Marine Corps and Coast Guard officers pursuing designation as Naval Aviators and Naval Flight Officers, the advanced training base for most Naval Flight Officers, and as the home base for the United States Navy Flight Demonstration Squadron, the precision-flying team known as the Blue Angels.

chunks.title: VS-32
chunks.text: VS-32, Sea Control Squadron 32, known as the "Maulers" was established as Composite Squadron 32 (VC-32) on 31 May 1949.

chunks.title: VS-32
chunks.text: It was redesignated Air Anti-Submarine Squadron 32 (VS-32) on 20 April 1950.

chunks.title: VS-32
chunks.text: The squadron initially flew the Grumman TBM-3E/-3W Avenger and was based at Naval Air Station Norfolk, Virginia.

chunks.title: VS-32
chunks.text: In 1951 the squadron moved to Naval Air Station Quonset Point, Rhode Island.

chunks.title: VS-32
chunks.text: VS-32 transitioned to the Grumman S2F-1 "Tracker" in 1954.

chunks.title: VS-32
chunks.text: The VS community moved in October 1973 to the homeport located at Naval Air Station Cecil Field, Florida.

chunks.title: VS-32
chunks.text: The squadron participated in Operation Desert Storm in 1991.

chunks.title: VS-32
chunks.text: Since the closing of NAS Cecil Field, the East coast VS Squadrons have moved to Naval Air Station Jacksonville in 1999.

chunks.title: VS-32
chunks.text: VS-32 was deactivated effective 30 September 2008 in a deactivation ceremony on 25 September.

chunks.title: Naval Air Facility Midway Island
chunks.text: Naval Air Station Midway Island, also known as NAS Midway, Naval Air Facility Midway, and NAF Midway (former ICAO PMDY), was a U.S. Naval Air Station in the Midway Atoll, the northernmost group of the Hawaiian archipelago.

chunks.title: Naval Air Facility Midway Island
chunks.text: It was in operation from 1941 to 1993, and played an important role in trans-Pacific aviation during those years.

chunks.title: Naval Air Facility Midway Island
chunks.text: Through its lifetime, the facility was variously designated as a Naval Air Station, a Naval Air Facility, and a naval base.

chunks.title: Naval Air Facility Midway Island
chunks.text: It was finally closed on 1 October 1993.

chunks.title: Aerodynamik

chunks.text: The 2004 Tour de France was a multiple stage bicycle race held from 3 to 25 July, and the 91st edition of the Tour de France.

chunks.title: 2004 Tour de France
chunks.text: It has no overall winner—although American cyclist Lance Armstrong originally won the event, the United States Anti-Doping Agency announced in August 2012 that they had disqualified Armstrong from all his results since 1998, including his seven Tour de France wins from 1999 to 2005; the Union Cycliste Internationale confirmed this verdict.

chunks.title: 1999 Tour de France
chunks.text: The 1999 Tour de France was a multiple stage bicycle race held from 3 to 25 July, and the 86th edition of the Tour de France.

chunks.title: 1999 Tour de France

chunks.title: 1999 Tour de France
chunks.text: There were no French stage winners for the first time since the 1926 Tour de France.

chunks.title: 1999 Tour de France
chunks.text: Additionally, Mario Cipollini won 4 stages in a row, setting the post-World War II record for consecutive stage wins (breaking the record of three, set by Gino Bartali in 1948.)

chunks.title: 2000 Tour de France
chunks.text: The 2000 Tour de France was a multiple stage bicycle race held from 1 to 23 July, and the 87th edition of the Tour de France.

chunks.title: 2000 Tour de France

chunks.title: Col de Sarenne
chunks.text: Col de Sarenne (1999 m ) is a mountain pass located in the Grandes Rousses massif, approximately 9 km east of Alpe d'Huez in the Isère department of France.

chunks.title: Col de Sarenne
chunks.text: The pass connects Alpe d'Huez with the villages of Mizoën and Le Freney-d'Oisans in the Romanche valley.

chunks.title: Col de Sarenne
chunks.text: The road over the pass was used on Stage 18 of the 2013 Tour de France bicycle race as this loops round to enable the cyclists to climb the Alpe d'Huez twice in the same stage.

chunks.title: 2003 Tour de France
chunks.text: The 2003 Tour de France was a multiple stage bicycle race held from 5 to 27 July, and the 90th edition of the Tour de France.

chunks.title: 2003 Tour de France
chunks.text: It has no overall winner—although American cyclist Lance Armstrong originally won the event, the United States Anti-Doping Agency announced in August 2012 that they had disqualified Armstrong from all his results since 1998, including his seven Tour de France wins from 1999 to 2005; the Union Cycliste Internationale has confirmed this verdict.

chunks.title: Rini Wagtmans
chunks.text: Marinus ("Rini") Wagtmans (born 26 December 1946 in Sint Willebrord) is a former Dutch professional road bicycle racer.

chunks.title: Rini Wagtmans
chunks.text: He was the nephew of Wout Wagtmans, a former professional who had won the Tour de Romandie stage race in 1952.

chunks.title: Rini Wagtmans
chunks.text: His father was a masseur while Tour de France stage winner Wim van Est was his neighbour.

chunks.title: Rini Wagtmans
chunks.text: In 1968 Rini turned professional.

chunks.title: Rini Wagtmans
chunks.text: The following year he finished third overall in the 1969 Vuelta a España.

chunks.title: Rini Wagtmans
chunks.text: He rode four editions of the Tour de France and won three stages, one in 1970, one in 1971 and one in 1972.

chunks.title: Rini Wagtmans
chunks.text: In the 1970 Tour de France he finished fifth overall.

chunks.title: Rini Wagtmans
chunks.text: In 1971 Tour de France while riding for Molteni, he wore the maillot jaune for one day but teammate and team leader Eddy Merckx took the jersey the following day.

chunks.title: Rini Wagtmans
chunks.text: He also won two stages in the 1970 Vuelta a España.

chunks.title: Rini Wagtmans
chunks.text: Wagtmans was known as one of the best descenders in the peloton and earned him the nickname "witte bles" which is translated as "white blaze".

chunks.title: Rini Wagtmans
chunks.text: Wagtmans ended his career early due to heart problems.

chunks.title: Rini Wagtmans
chunks.text: Afterwards he was a cycling coach, a member for the Royal Dutch Cycling Union, and then a successful businessman.

chunks.title: Rini Wagtmans
chunks.text: In 2005, Wagtmans became a ridder or Dutch knight in the Order of Orange-Nassau.

chunks.title: Rini Wagtmans
chunks.text: In 2006, Wagtmans’ biography was published.

chunks.title: 2002 Tour de France

chunks.title: Tour de France Soundtracks

chunks.title: Tour de France Soundtracks

chunks.text: The album was recorded for the 100th anniversary of the first "Tour de France" bicycle race, although it missed its intended release date for the actual tour.

chunks.title: Tour de France Soundtracks

chunks.text: The announcement of the release caused much anticipation, as it had been 17 years since the group had put out a full album of new studio material (1986's "Electric Café", also known as "Techno Pop").

chunks.title: Whitechapel (band)
chunks.text: Whitechapel is an American deathcore band from Knoxville, Tennessee.

chunks.title: Whitechapel (band)
chunks.text: The band is named after the Whitechapel district in East London, England, referencing the series of murders committed by Jack the Ripper.

chunks.title: Whitechapel (band)
chunks.text: The group comprises vocalist Phil Bozeman, guitarists Ben Savage, Alex Wade, and Zach Householder, bassist Gabe Crisp, and drummer Ben Harclerode.

chunks.title: Whitechapel (band)
chunks.text: Founded in 2006 by Bozeman and Savage, the band has released six studio albums, eleven music videos and are currently signed to Metal Blade Records.

chunks.title: Whitechapel (band)
chunks.text: Whitechapel's 2010 album "A New Era of Corruption", sold around 10,600 copies in the United States in its first week of release and debuted at position No. 43 on the "Billboard" 200 chart.

chunks.title: Whitechapel (band)
chunks.text: The band's self-titled fourth album was released on June 19, 2012 and debuted at No. 47 on the Billboard 200, selling roughly 9,200 copies in its first week.

chunks.title: Whitechapel (band)
chunks.text: In 2014 the band released their fifth full-length album, "Our Endless War" to generally positive reviews.

chunks.title: Whitechapel (band)
chunks.text: The album sold roughly 16,000 copies in its first week and debuted at no. 10 on the Billbord 200.

chunks.title: Whitechapel (band)
chunks.text: They released their sixth full-length album Mark of the Blade in 2016 to greater critical acclaim, selling roughly 8,000 copies in the first week of its release.

chunks.title: Moving On (Asking Alexandria song)
chunks.text: Moving On is a power ballad by English Metalcore band Asking Alexandria.

chunks.title: Moving On (Asking Alexandria song)
chunks.text: It was released on July 29, 2014.

chunks.title: Moving On (Asking Alexandria song)
chunks.text: It is the band's last single before the departure of vocalist Danny Worsnop in January 2015.

chunks.title: I Won't Give In
chunks.text: "I Won't Give In" is a song by British metalcore band Asking Alexandria, released on 26 May 2015 as the first single from their fourth studio album "The Black".

chunks.title: I Won't Give In
chunks.text: It marks the first song featuring new frontman Denis Stoff after the departure of former vocalist Danny Worsnop in January 2015.

chunks.title: From Death to Destiny
chunks.text: From Death to Destiny is the third studio album by British metalcore band Asking Alexandria.

chunks.title: From Death to Destiny
chunks.text: The band released the first single titled "Run Free" on 13 August 2012, via the Sumerian Records YouTube page.

chunks.title: From Death to Destiny
chunks.text: The second single titled "The Death of Me", which had been teased several times by band members and a third track on the new album/single "Killing You", Sumerian alike through various social media sites, was released on 28 March 2013, again via the Sumerian Records YouTube page.

chunks.title: From Death to Destiny
chunks.text: The live premiere took place the same day, at a performance at the Nile Theatre in Mesa, Arizona.

chunks.title: From Death to Destiny
chunks.text: Sources say that the track "Run Free" will be different on "From Death to Destiny" than the version released on "".

chunks.title: From Death to Destiny
chunks.text: The album was released on 6 August 2013.

chunks.title: From Death to Destiny
chunks.text: This is the last album to feature original lead vocalist Danny Worsnop until his return in October 2016.

chunks.title: Asking Alexandria
chunks.text: Asking Alexandria are an English rock band from York, North Yorkshire consisting of lead vocalist Danny Worsnop, guitarists Ben Bruce and Cameron Liddell, drummer James Cassells and bassist Sam Bettley.

chunks.title: Stand Up and Scream
chunks.text: Stand Up and Scream is the debut studio album by English metalcore band Asking Alexandria, released on 15 September 2009 through Sumerian Records.

chunks.title: Stand Up and Scream
chunks.text: The album has charted at number 170 on the Billboard 200, number 29 on Top Independent albums, and number 5 on Top Heatseekers.

chunks.title: Stand Up and Scream
chunks.text: The record managed to remain at the Top Heatseekers chart at position number 36 until the end of July 2010.

chunks.title: Stand Up and Scream
chunks.text: The album received mixed to positive reviews from critics, with Danny Worsnop's unclean vocals, and the loud guitars and drums being praised.

chunks.title: Stand Up and Scream
chunks.text: However, the lyrics, Worsnop's clean vocals and electronic elements were subject of criticism.

chunks.title: Stand Up and Scream
chunks.text: The album has gone on to sell over 100,000 copies worldwide.

chunks.title: Ben Bruce
chunks.text: Benjamin Paul "Ben" Bruce (born 31 October 1988) is an English musician.

chunks.title: Ben Bruce
chunks.text: He is a solo artist and also the lead guitarist and backing vocalist of metalcore band Asking Alexandria.

chunks.title: Ben Bruce
chunks.text: Bruce co-founded the band with lead vocalist Danny Worsnop.

chunks.title: Killing You
chunks.text: Killing You is a song by English Metalcore band Asking Alexandria.

chunks.title: Killing You
chunks.text: It is the band's second single from their third studio album, "From Death to Destiny".

chunks.title: Killing You
chunks.text: The single was released on 16 July 2013.

chunks.title: The Dillinger Escape Plan discography
chunks.text: The discography of The Dillinger Escape Plan, an American mathcore band, consists of six studio albums, six extended plays (EPs), two split EPs, eight singles, one video album, 15 music videos and seven other appearances.

chunks.title: The Dillinger Escape Plan discography
chunks.text: Formed in Morris Plains, New Jersey in 1997, the band originally featured vocalist Dimitri Minakakis, guitarists Ben Weinman and Derek Brantley, bassist Adam Doll and drummer Chris Pennie; Brantley left after two shows and was replaced briefly by touring guitarist John Fulton, who himself left in 1998.

chunks.title: The Dillinger Escape Plan discography
chunks.text: In 1997 the band released its self-titled debut EP on New Jersey independent label Now or Never Records, after which they were signed by Relapse Records who issued their second EP "Under the Running Board" in 1998.

chunks.title: The Dillinger Escape Plan discography
chunks.text: The EP charted on the UK Singles Chart, reaching number 194.

chunks.title: The Black (Asking Alexandria album)
chunks.text: The Black is the fourth studio album by English rock band Asking Alexandria.

chunks.title: The Black (Asking Alexandria album)
chunks.text: It was released on 25 March 2016, and is their first and only album to feature second lead vocalist Denis Stoff, who replaced original lead vocalist Danny Worsnop.

chunks.title: The Black (Asking Alexandria album)
chunks.text: Worsnop returned to the band in October of 2016.

chunks.title: The Black (Asking Alexandria album)
chunks.text: The album was preceded by the singles "I Won't Give In" released on 26 May 2015, "Undivided" released on 25 September 2015, and the album's eponymous track "The Black" released on 2 February 2016.

chunks.title: The Black (Asking Alexandria album)
chunks.text: The first song on the album, "Let It Sleep", was released on 3 March 2016, with a music video for the track being released the following day.

chunks.title: David Tisch
chunks.text: David Tisch (born 1981) is a businessman and angel investor based in New York City.

chunks.title: David Tisch
chunks.text: He is managing partner of BoxGroup, a seed-stage capital firm, and a co-founder of TechStars New York City.

chunks.title: David Tisch
chunks.text: He is the grandson of American businessman Laurence Tisch, co-owner of Loews Corporation.

chunks.title: David Tisch
chunks.text: His great-uncle, Preston Robert Tisch purchased the New York Giants, now co-owned by Steve Tisch, who produced the films "Forrest Gump" and "Risky Business".

chunks.title: Jonathan Tisch
chunks.text: Jonathan Tisch is Chairman Emeritus of the "United States Travel Association" (U.S. Travel), a travel industry lobbying group, a trustee of Tufts University, and a board member of the Tribeca Film Institute.

chunks.title: Jonathan Tisch
chunks.text: He is a co-owner, a member of the board of directors, and treasurer of the New York Football Giants.

chunks.title: Jonathan Tisch
chunks.text: He served as co-chairman of the 2014 NY/NJ Super Bowl Host Committee.

chunks.title: Dave Jennings (American football)
chunks.text: David Tuthill "Dave" Jennings (June 8, 1952 – June 19, 2013) was an American football punter who played in the National Football League (NFL) from 1974 to 1987.

chunks.title: Dave Jennings (American football)
chunks.text: He played for the New York Giants and the New York Jets.

chunks.title: Dave Jennings (American football)
chunks.text: He worked as a radio color commentator for Giants games from 2002 until 2007, when he was replaced by former Giants linebacker Carl Banks.

chunks.title: Dave Jennings (American football)
chunks.text: He had also worked as a radio commentator for Jets games from 1988 to 2001.

chunks.title: Dave Jennings (American football)
chunks.text: Jennings worked as a game analyst alongside WFAN Giants announcers Bob Papa and Dick Lynch.

chunks.title: Dave Jennings (American football)
chunks.text: In addition to his booth work, Jennings was a part of the Giants pre and post game shows, covering player interviews from the locker room.

chunks.title: Dave Jennings (American football)
chunks.text: Jennings, who had Parkinson's disease, left broadcasting altogether following the 2008 season.

chunks.title: AT&T Park
chunks.text: AT&T Park is a baseball park located in the South Beach neighborhood of San Francisco, California.

chunks.title: AT&T Park
chunks.text: Since 2000, it has served as the home of the San Francisco Giants, the city's Major League Baseball (MLB) franchise.

chunks.title: AT&T Park
chunks.text: Originally named Pacific Bell Park, then SBC Park in 2003 after SBC Communications acquired Pacific Bell, the stadium was ultimately christened AT&T Park in 2006, following SBC's buyout of AT&T.

chunks.title: AT&T Park
chunks.text: The park stands along the San Francisco Bay, a segment of which is named McCovey Cove in honor of former Giants player Willie McCovey.

chunks.title: Laurence Tisch
chunks.text: Laurence Alan "Larry" Tisch (March 5, 1923 – November 15, 2003) was an American businessman, Wall Street investor and billionaire.

chunks.title: Laurence Tisch
chunks.text: He was the CEO of CBS television network from 1986 to 1995.

chunks.title: Laurence Tisch
chunks.text: With his brother Bob Tisch, he was part owner of the Loews Corporation.

chunks.title: Osi Umenyiora
chunks.text: Ositadimma "Osi" Umenyiora (born November 16, 1981) is a British sports pundit and former American Football defensive end who played in the National Football League (NFL).

chunks.title: Osi Umenyiora
chunks.text: He played college football for Troy University and was drafted by the New York Giants in the second round of the 2003 NFL Draft.

chunks.title: Osi Umenyiora
chunks.text: Umenyiora was a two-time Pro Bowl selection and holds the Giants franchise record for most sacks in one game.

chunks.title: Osi Umenyiora
chunks.text: He is one of four British-born players to have won a Super Bowl, joining Marvin Allen, Scott McCready and former Giants teammate Lawrence Tynes.

chunks.title: Andrew Tisch
chunks.text: Andrew Tisch is the co-chair of Loews Corporation, the company founded by his father Larry Tisch and uncle Bob Tisch.

chunks.title: Andrew Tisch
chunks.text: Together with his brother, James S. Tisch, and his first cousin, Jonathan Tisch, Andrew oversees a holding company involved in hotels, oil, and insurance.

chunks.title: Andrew Tisch
chunks.text: His mother is Wilma "Billie" Stein.

chunks.title: The Testimony (2015 film)
chunks.text: The Testimony is a 2015 American short-documentary film which chronicles the largest rape tribunal in the history of the Democratic Republic of the Congo as a result of M23 rebellion fighting.

chunks.title: The Testimony (2015 film)
chunks.text: It is directed and shot by Vanessa Block and produced by Block, Steve Tisch, Mitchell Block and Michael Sarnoski.

chunks.title: The Testimony (2015 film)
chunks.text: "The Testimony " was shortlisted with ten other documentaries from 74 entries submitted to the 88th Academy Awards in Documentary Short Subject category.

chunks.title: The Testimony (2015 film)
chunks.text: The final five nominations are scheduled to be announced on January 14, 2016.

chunks.title: Steve Tisch
chunks.text: Steven Elliot Tisch (born February 14, 1949) is an American film producer and businessman.

chunks.title: Steve Tisch
chunks.text: He is the chairman and Executive Vice President of the New York Giants, the NFL team co-owned by his family, as well as a film and television producer.

chunks.title: Steve Tisch
chunks.text: He is the son of former Giants co-owner Bob Tisch.

chunks.title: SSC Yugal
chunks.text: Sydney Soccer Club Yugal is a defunct association football club from Sydney, Australia.

chunks.title: SSC Yugal
chunks.text: The club, formed by Yugoslav immigrants in the mid-1950s, was originally known as Dalmatinac due to the Dalmatian origins of most of its founders.

chunks.title: SSC Yugal
chunks.text: It competed initially in the Granville District competition before joining the New South Wales Federation of Soccer Club's Second Division Competition in 1958, the same year as other former giants of soccer in New South Wales, Pan-Hellenic, later known as Sydney Olympic FC and Polonia.

chunks.title: Sticky bomb
chunks.text: The Grenade, Hand, Anti-Tank No. 74, commonly known as the S.T. Grenade or sticky bomb, was a British hand grenade designed and produced during the Second World War.

chunks.title: Sticky bomb
chunks.text: The grenade was one of a number of anti-tank weapons developed for use by the British Army and Home Guard as an "ad hoc" solution to a lack of sufficient anti-tank guns in the aftermath of the Dunkirk evacuation.

chunks.title: Sticky bomb
chunks.text: Designed by a team from MIR(c) including Major Millis Jefferis and Stuart Macrae, the grenade consisted of a glass sphere containing an explosive made of nitroglycerin and additives (this added stability to the mix, as well as giving it its squash-head-like effect) covered in a strong adhesive and surrounded by a sheet-metal casing.

chunks.title: Sticky bomb
chunks.text: When the user pulled a pin on the handle of the grenade, the casing would fall away and expose the sticky sphere.

chunks.title: Sticky bomb
chunks.text: Pulling another pin would arm the firing mechanism and the user would then attempt to attach the grenade to an enemy tank or other vehicle.

chunks.title: Sticky bomb
chunks.text: Letting go of the handle would release a lever that would activate a five-second fuse, which would then detonate the nitroglycerin.

chunks.title: Model 17 grenade
chunks.text: The Model 17 Eierhandgranate ("Egg grenade") is a small defensive and offensive hand grenade which was used by Germany during World War I.

chunks.title: Model 17 grenade
chunks.text: The average soldier could throw it 40 meters or farther.

chunks.title: Model 17 grenade
chunks.text: It was more portable than the heavier Kugelhandgranate and less awkward to handle than the Stick grenade.

chunks.title: Model 17 grenade
chunks.text: The body of the grenade was initially smooth and thus difficult to hold so the design was modified with the addition of a raised band to provide better grip.

chunks.title: Model 1914 grenade
chunks.text: The Model 1914 grenade ("Ручная граната образца 1914 года" > "Ruchnaya granata obraztsa 1914 goda", "Hand Grenade Pattern of year 1914") is a Russian stick concussion grenade (fragmentation grenade via an optional jacket) that was used during World War I and World War II.

chunks.title: M34 grenade
chunks.text: The M34 White Phosphorus Smoke Grenade or "Willie Pete" was a chemical grenade manufactured by Rocky Mountain Arsenal from the late 1950s and used by U.S. forces during the Vietnam War and was also used during the First Gulf War.

chunks.title: M34 grenade
chunks.text: The M34 WP Grenade replaced the World War II M15 WP grenade.

chunks.title: M34 grenade
chunks.text: The M34 could be fired from a rifle grenade launcher using M2-series grenade launching adapters, which the groove around the tapered base allowing the adapter arms to grasp it.

chunks.title: M34 grenade
chunks.text: The M15 could not be fired as a rifle grenade.

chunks.title: M34 grenade
chunks.text: The M34 had a segmented body to allow for a better hand grip and to identify it as a casualty-producing grenade, even though it did not fragment.

chunks.title: M34 grenade
chunks.text: The smooth-bodied M15 was sometimes assumed to be a burning type smoke grenade as the AN-M8 white smoke and resulted in injuries.

chunks.title: Type 98 grenade
chunks.text: The Type 98 Hand Grenade (九八式柄付手榴弾 , Kyūhachi-shiki etsuki teryūdan ) was a fragmentation hand grenade deployed by the Imperial Japanese Army during World War II.

chunks.title: Type 98 grenade
chunks.text: The explosive charge contained 3 oz (85 g) of picric acid (more powerful but less safe explosive than TNT).

chunks.title: Type 98 grenade
chunks.text: The weapon operated identically to the Type 23 (Chinese version of the German Model 24) stick grenade on which it was based, except that a pull ring was attached to the igniting cord, and the actual fuse delay itself was reduced to four to five seconds (varying from grenade to grenade).

chunks.title: M7 grenade launcher
chunks.text: The M7 grenade launcher, formally rifle grenade launcher, M7, was a 22 mm rifle grenade launcher attachment for the M1 Garand rifle that saw widespread use throughout World War II and the Korean War.

chunks.title: M7 grenade launcher
chunks.text: The M7 was a tube-shaped device, with one end slotting over the barrel of the rifle, the other end holding the grenade in place.

chunks.title: M7 grenade launcher
chunks.text: Blank cartridges were loaded into the rifle prior to firing.

chunks.title: M7 grenade launcher
chunks.text: When fired, the expanding gases generated by the cartridges propelled the grenade forward with considerable force.

chunks.title: M7 grenade launcher
chunks.text: The M7 could fire grenades up to 350 m , compared with the maximum of 30 m achieved by hand grenades.

chunks.title: Offensive grenade wz. 24
chunks.text: The Granat zaczepny wz.24 (Polish for "Offensive grenade, Mark 1924") was a concussion grenade used by the Polish Army before and during World War II.

chunks.title: Offensive grenade wz. 24
chunks.text: The oval egg-shaped shell casing was made of thin sheet metal filled with picric acid or TNT.

chunks.title: Offensive grenade wz. 24
chunks.text: Initially used with a variety of fuses, since early 1930s the grenade was used with the standard Zapalnik wz.

chunks.title: Offensive grenade wz. 24
chunks.text: Gr.

chunks.title: Offensive grenade wz. 24
chunks.text: 31 time fuse designed for the Defensive grenade wz.33.

chunks.title: Offensive grenade wz. 24
chunks.text: The grenade armed with the wz.

chunks.title: Offensive grenade wz. 24
chunks.text: Gr.

chunks.title: Offensive grenade wz. 24
chunks.text: 31 fuse is sometimes referred to as wz.

chunks.title: Offensive grenade wz. 24
chunks.text: 24/31 to distinguish it from the original wz.24 grenade armed with different fuses.

chunks.title: Stielhandgranate
chunks.text: The Stielhandgranate (Literally, German for "stalk hand grenade") was a German hand grenade of unique design.

chunks.title: Stielhandgranate
chunks.text: It was the standard issue of the German Empire during World War I and World War II in which became the infamously issue of Nazi Germany's Wehrmacht.

chunks.title: Stielhandgranate
chunks.text: The very distinctive appearance led to it being called a "stick grenade", or "potato masher" in British Army slang, and is today one of the most easily recognized infantry weapons of the 20th century.

chunks.title: M1 Grenade Adapter
chunks.text: The Grenade Projection Adapter was an expedient rifle grenade used by the American Military in World War II, Korea, and Vietnam.

chunks.title: M1 Grenade Adapter
chunks.text: It consisted of an add-on 22mm stabilizer tube and fins that converted a hand-grenade into a rifle grenade.

chunks.title: M1 Grenade Adapter
chunks.text: It was supplemented by the M17 rifle grenade, and eventually made obsolete by the 40 mm M79 grenade launcher.

chunks.title: Hawkins grenade
chunks.text: The Grenade, Hand, Anti-tank, No. 75, also known as the Hawkins grenade was a British anti-tank hand grenade used during World War II.

chunks.title: Hawkins grenade
chunks.text: It was one of a number of grenades developed for use by the British Army and Home Guard in the aftermath of the Dunkirk evacuation.

chunks.title: Hawkins grenade
chunks.text: The grenade first appeared in 1942, and was designed to be more versatile than previous grenades, such as the Grenade, Hand, Anti-tank No. 73 and the Grenade, Hand, Anti-Tank, No. 74.

chunks.title: Alois Brunner
chunks.text: Alois Brunner (8 April 1912 – 2001 or 2010) was an Austrian "Schutzstaffel" (SS) officer who worked as Adolf Eichmann's assistant.

chunks.title: Alois Brunner
chunks.text: Brunner is held responsible for sending over 100,000 European Jews to ghettos and internment camps in eastern Europe.

chunks.title: Alois Brunner
chunks.text: He was commander of the Drancy internment camp outside Paris from June 1943 to August 1944, from which nearly 24,000 people were deported.

chunks.title: Bill Young (CIA officer)
chunks.text: William (Bill) Young (28 October 1934 – 1 April 2011) was a Central Intelligence Agency paramilitary officer born in Berkeley, California and raised in Burma and Thailand.

chunks.title: Bill Young (CIA officer)
chunks.text: Although he was Caucasian, he was reared in the local hill tribe culture.

chunks.title: Bill Young (CIA officer)
chunks.text: Because his father and brother already worked for the CIA and knew Bill Lair, the Agency knew of his extensive cultural contacts with the Lahu people and other Southeast Asian hill tribes.

chunks.title: Bill Young (CIA officer)
chunks.text: With command of several Asian languages, he was made a natural recruiter of local guerrillas for the CIA's covert operations in the secret war in the Kingdom of Laos.

chunks.title: Bill Young (CIA officer)
chunks.text: He was then considered for the position of case officer to Hmong Vang Pao.

chunks.title: Bill Young (CIA officer)
chunks.text: He was passed over in favor of sending him on an extended reconnaissance of the Kingdom of Laos.

chunks.title: Bill Young (CIA officer)
chunks.text: His tour ranged westward from his start at Long Tieng—which he reported as well-sited for operations in the Plain of Jars—back to familiar territory in the Golden Triangle.

chunks.title: Thomas Conover
chunks.text: Thomas H. Conover was a United States Navy officer born in New Jersey in 1794.

chunks.title: Thomas Conover
chunks.text: He entered the Navy as a midshipman January 1, 1812 and during his fifty-three years of service to the Navy would serve aboard the "Essex" , "Guerriere" , "John Adams" and was Captain of the  during her service with the African Squadron.

chunks.title: Thomas Conover
chunks.text: He was one of the first officers to be promoted to the rank of Commodore on July 16, 1862.

chunks.title: Thomas Conover
chunks.text: Conover died on September 25, 1864.

chunks.title: Karl Diebitsch
chunks.text: Karl Diebitsch (3 January 1899 – 6 August 1985) was an artist and the Schutzstaffel (SS) officer responsible for designing much of the SS regalia in the Third Reich, including the chained SS officer's dagger scabbard.

chunks.title: Karl Diebitsch
chunks.text: Diebitsch worked with graphic designer Walter Heck to draft the well-known all-black SS uniform.

chunks.title: Karl Diebitsch
chunks.text: Also with his business partner, industrialist Franz Nagy, Diebitsch began the production of art porcelain at the factory Porzellan Manufaktur Allach.

chunks.title: Dienstalterslisten der SS
chunks.text: The SS-Dienstalterslisten (in German: "Dienstaltersliste der Schutzstaffel der NSDAP"; English: SS Officers list ) was an official listing of all SS officers of the middle and higher officer corps.

chunks.title: Dienstalterslisten der SS
chunks.text: They appeared in book form.

chunks.title: Karl Freiherr Michel von Tüßling
chunks.text: Karl Freiherr Michel von Tüßling (27 July 1907 – 30 October 1991) was a Schutzstaffel (SS) officer who served in the Nazi government of German dictator Adolf Hitler and in the SS Main Office.

chunks.title: Karl Freiherr Michel von Tüßling
chunks.text: From 1936 onwards, he was the personal adjutant of "Reichsleiter" and SS-"Obergruppenführer" Philipp Bouhler, who was in charge of Hitler's Chancellery (Kanzlei des Führers), head of the euthanasia programme Aktion T4, as well as co-initiator of Aktion 14f13.

chunks.title: Karl Freiherr Michel von Tüßling
chunks.text: In 1947 Tüßling provided an affidavit in defence of war criminal Viktor Brack who was sentenced to death at the Nuremberg trials.

chunks.title: Róger David Torres Mendoza
chunks.text: Róger David Torres Mendoza is a Peruvian Police officer born on January 26 in the resort of Buenos Aires located in Victor Larco, La Libertad Region, and in January 2012 he was appointed by the Ministry of Interior of the Peruvian government as head of the Direction Territorial of Police of La Libertad (DIRTEPOL) based in the city of Trujillo.

chunks.title: Runic insignia of the Schutzstaffel
chunks.text: The runic insignia of the "Schutzstaffel" (known in German as the "SS-Runen") were used from the 1920s to 1945 on "Schutzstaffel" flags, uniforms and other items as symbols of various aspects of Nazi ideology and Germanic mysticism.

chunks.title: Runic insignia of the Schutzstaffel
chunks.text: They also represented virtues seen as desirable in SS members, and were based on "völkisch" mystic Guido von List's Armanen runes, which he loosely based on the historical runic alphabets. SS runes are commonly used by members of the neo-nazis.

chunks.title: Esther Schapira
chunks.text: Schapira is co-author of "The Act of Alois Brunner", and producer of two award-winning documentaries, "Drei Kugeln und ein totes Kind" ("Three bullets and a dead child") (2002), about the death of Muhammad al-Durrah in Gaza in 2000, and "Der Tag, als Theo van Gogh ermordet wurde" ("The day Theo van Gogh was murdered") (2007), about the killing in 2004 of Dutch filmmaker, Theo van Gogh.

chunks.title: Esther Schapira
chunks.text: The latter won her and her co-producer, Kamil Taylan, a Prix Europa award.

chunks.title: Esther Schapira
chunks.text: In 2009, she produced a second documentary about the death of al-Durrah, "Das Kind, Der Tod, und Die Wahrheit" ("The Child, the Death, and the Truth").

chunks.title: Fridolin Glass
chunks.text: Fridolin Glass, also Glaß (born 14 December 1910 in Lemberg – died 21 February 1943 in the Soviet Union) was an Austrian Nazi activist and Schutzstaffel (SS) officer.

chunks.title: Fridolin Glass
chunks.text: Glass came to prominence in 1934 when he became the effective leader of the July Putsch, a failed coup attempt by the Nazis in Austria.

chunks.title: Crickets as pets
chunks.text: Keeping crickets as pets emerged in China in early antiquity.

chunks.title: Crickets as pets
chunks.text: Initially, crickets were kept for their "songs" (stridulation).

chunks.title: Crickets as pets
chunks.text: In the early 12th century the Chinese people began holding cricket fights.

chunks.title: Crickets as pets
chunks.text: Throughout the Imperial era the Chinese also kept pet cicadas and grasshoppers, but crickets were the favorites in the Forbidden City and with the commoners alike.

chunks.title: Crickets as pets
chunks.text: The art of selecting and breeding the finest fighting crickets was perfected during the Qing dynasty and remained a monopoly of the imperial court until the beginning of the 19th century.

chunks.title: Jicheng (Beijing)
chunks.text: Ji (蓟/薊 Jì), Jicheng or the City of Ji (蓟城/薊城 Jìchéng) was an ancient city in northern China, which has become the longest continuously inhabited section of modern Beijing.

chunks.title: Jicheng (Beijing)
chunks.text: Historical mention of Ji dates to the founding of the Zhou Dynasty in about 1045 BC.

chunks.title: Jicheng (Beijing)
chunks.text: Archaeological finds in southwestern Beijing where Ji was believed to be located date to the Spring and Autumn period (771-476 BC).

chunks.title: Jicheng (Beijing)
chunks.text: The City of Ji served as the capital of the ancient states of Ji and Yan until the unification of China by the Qin Dynasty in 221 BC.

chunks.title: Jicheng (Beijing)
chunks.text: Thereafter, the city was a prefectural capital for Youzhou through the Han Dynasty, Three Kingdoms, Western Jin Dynasty, Sixteen Kingdoms, Northern Dynasties, and Sui Dynasty.

chunks.title: Jicheng (Beijing)
chunks.text: With the creation of a Jizhou (蓟州) during the Tang Dynasty in what is now Tianjin Municipality, the City of Ji took on the name Youzhou.

chunks.title: Jicheng (Beijing)
chunks.text: Youzhou was one of the Sixteen Prefectures ceded to the Khitans during the Five Dynasties.

chunks.title: Jicheng (Beijing)
chunks.text: The city then became the southern capital of the Liao Dynasty and then main capital of the Jin Dynasty (1115-1234).

chunks.title: Jicheng (Beijing)
chunks.text: In the 13th Century, Kublai Khan built a new capital city for the Yuan Dynasty adjacent to Ji to the north.

chunks.title: Jicheng (Beijing)
chunks.text: The old city of Ji became a suburb to Dadu.

chunks.title: Jicheng (Beijing)
chunks.text: In the Ming Dynasty, the old and new cities were merged by Beijing's Ming-era city wall.

chunks.title: Silla–Tang War
chunks.text: The Silla–Tang War occurred in the 7th century between the Korean Silla Kingdom and its newly conquered vassals Goguryeo and Baekje (commonly referred to as Unified Silla), and the Chinese Tang dynasty that began in the geopolitical context immediately following the conquest of Goguryeo and Baekje by Silla and Tang Dynasty.

chunks.title: Koyasan Reihōkan
chunks.text: Shōchi-in (正智院 ) and Hōju-in (宝寿院 ) own Japanese manuscripts of parts of the Wenguan Cilin (文館詞林 , Bunkan shirin , lit.

chunks.title: Koyasan Reihōkan
chunks.text: "Forest of officials' poems and prose") , a Tang Dynasty imperial poetry collection.

chunks.title: Koyasan Reihōkan
chunks.text: Other manuscripts of this work had been lost in China as early as 9th century.

chunks.title: Koyasan Reihōkan

chunks.title: History of ecology
chunks.text: Ecology is a new science and considered as an important branch of biological science, having only become prominent during the second half of the 20th century.

chunks.title: History of ecology
chunks.text: Ecological thought is derivative of established currents in philosophy, particularly from ethics and politics.

chunks.title: History of ecology
chunks.text: Its history stems all the way back to the 4th century.

chunks.title: History of ecology
chunks.text: One of the first ecologists whose writings survive may have been Aristotle or perhaps his student, Theophrastus, both of whom had interest in many species of animals and plants.

chunks.title: History of ecology
chunks.text: Theophrastus described interrelationships between animals and their environment as early as the 4th century BC.

chunks.title: History of ecology
chunks.text: Ecology developed substantially in the 18th and 19th century.

chunks.title: History of ecology
chunks.text: It began with Carl Linnaeus and his work with the economy of nature.

chunks.title: History of ecology
chunks.text: Soon after came Alexander von Humboldt and his work with botanical geography.

chunks.title: History of ecology
chunks.text: Alfred Russel Wallace and Karl Möbius then contributed with the notion of biocoenosis.

chunks.title: History of ecology
chunks.text: Eugenius Warming’s work with ecological plant geography led to the founding of ecology as a discipline.

chunks.title: History of ecology
chunks.text: Charles Darwin’s work also contributed to the science of ecology, and Darwin is often attributed with progressing the discipline more than anyone else in its young history.

chunks.title: History of ecology
chunks.text: Ecological thought expanded even more in the early 20th century.

chunks.title: History of ecology
chunks.text: Major contributions included: Eduard Suess’ and Vladimir Vernadsky’s work with the biosphere, Arthur Tansley’s ecosystem, Charles Elton's "Animal Ecology", and Henry Cowles ecological succession.

chunks.title: History of ecology
chunks.text: Ecology influenced the social sciences and humanities.

chunks.title: History of ecology
chunks.text: Human ecology began in the early 20th century and it recognized humans as an ecological factor.

chunks.title: History of ecology
chunks.text: Later James Lovelock advanced views on earth as a macro-organism with the Gaia hypothesis.

chunks.title: History of ecology
chunks.text: Conservation stemmed from the science of ecology.

chunks.title: History of ecology
chunks.text: Important figures and movements include Shelford and the ESA, National Environmental Policy act, George Perkins Marsh, Theodore Roosevelt, Stephen A. Forbes, and post-Dust Bowl conservation.

chunks.title: History of ecology
chunks.text: Later in the 20th century world governments collaborated on man’s effects on the biosphere and Earth’s environment.

chunks.title: History of gunpowder
chunks.text: Gunpowder is the first physical explosive and propellant.

chunks.title: History of gunpowder
chunks.text: Before its invention, many incendiary and burning devices had been used, including Greek fire.

chunks.title: History of gunpowder
chunks.text: The invention of gunpowder is usually attributed to experimentation in Chinese alchemy by Taoists in the pursuit of immortality, and is popularly listed as one of the "Four Great Inventions" of China.

chunks.title: History of gunpowder
chunks.text: It was invented during the late Tang dynasty (9th century) but the earliest record of a written formula appeared in the Song dynasty (11th century).

chunks.title: History of gunpowder
chunks.text: Knowledge of gunpowder spread rapidly throughout the Old World possibly as a result of the Mongol conquests during the 13th century, with the earliest written formula for it outside of China contained within the Opus Majus, a 1267 treatise by the English friar Roger Bacon.

chunks.title: History of gunpowder
chunks.text: It was employed in warfare to some effect from at least the 12th century in weapons such as fire arrows, bombs, and the fire lance before the appearance of the gun.

chunks.title: History of gunpowder
chunks.text: While the fire lance was eventually supplanted by the gun, other gunpowder weapons such as rockets continued to see use in China, Korea, India, and eventually Europe.

chunks.title: History of gunpowder
chunks.text: Bombs too never ceased to develop and continued to progress into the modern day as grenades, mines, and other explosive implements.

chunks.title: History of gunpowder
chunks.text: Gunpowder has also been used for non-military purposes such as fireworks for entertainment, or in explosives for mining and tunneling.

chunks.title: Cricket fighting
chunks.text: Cricket fighting is a blood sport involving the fighting of male crickets.

chunks.title: Cricket fighting
chunks.text: Unlike most blood sports such as bullfighting and cockfighting, cricket fighting rarely causes injuries to the animals.

chunks.title: Cricket fighting
chunks.text: It is a popular pastime in China and dates back more than 1,000 years to the Tang Dynasty.

chunks.title: Cricket fighting
chunks.text: However, the sport has been losing its popularity in China.

chunks.title: Gautama Siddha
chunks.text: Gautama Siddha, (fl.

chunks.title: Gautama Siddha
chunks.text: 8th century) astronomer, astrologer and compiler of Indian descent, known for leading the compilation of the "Treatise on Astrology of the Kaiyuan Era" during the Tang Dynasty.

chunks.title: Gautama Siddha
chunks.text: He was born in Chang'an, and his family was originally from India, according to a tomb stele uncovered in 1977 in Xi'an.

chunks.title: Gautama Siddha
chunks.text: The Gautama family had probably settled in China over many generations, and might have been present in China prior even to the foundation of the Tang Dynasty.

chunks.title: Gautama Siddha
chunks.text: He was most notable for his translation of Navagraha calendar into Chinese.

chunks.title: Gautama Siddha
chunks.text: He also introduced Indian numerals with zero (〇) in 718 in China as a replacement of counting rods.

chunks.title: Tang dynasty in Inner Asia
chunks.text: The Tang dynasty in Inner Asia was the expansion of the Tang dynasty's realm in the Inner Asia in the 7th and, to a lesser degree, the 8th century AD, in the Tarim Basin, across the Gobi Desert and into Middle Asia.

chunks.title: Tang dynasty in Inner Asia
chunks.text: Wars were fought against the Gokturk Empires and Xueyantuo, but also against the states of the Tarim basin.

chunks.title: Tang dynasty in Inner Asia
chunks.text: This expansion was not steady; for example, the Tang did lose control of the Tarim basin temporarily to the Tibetans in the 680s, and their expansion north of the Gobi was thwarted in 682.

chunks.title: Tang dynasty in Inner Asia
chunks.text: Emperor Taizong's military success was, in part, a consequence of changes he initiated in the Chinese army, including improved weaponry.

chunks.title: Tang dynasty in Inner Asia
chunks.text: The emperor placed a new emphasis on cavalry, which was very important because his non-Chinese opponents used the horse effectively in warfare.

chunks.title: Shanhua Temple
chunks.text: Shanhua Temple () is a Buddhist temple located in Datong, Shanxi Province, China.

chunks.title: Shanhua Temple
chunks.text: The temple was first founded during the early 8th century of the Tang Dynasty, but its earliest surviving building dates from the 11th century.

chunks.title: Shanhua Temple
chunks.text: The temple was heavily repaired over the years, and today three original halls and two recently rebuilt pavilions survive.

chunks.title: Shanhua Temple
chunks.text: The largest, and earliest hall, dating from the 11th-century Liao Dynasty, is the Mahavira Hall and is one of the largest of its kind in China.

chunks.title: Shanhua Temple
chunks.text: Also historically significant are the Main Gate and Sansheng Hall, both dating from 12th century during the Jin dynasty.

chunks.title: Sue Ennis
chunks.text: Sue Ennis is a Seattle songwriter whose songs include Classic Rock radio staples "Straight On", "Even It Up" and "Dog & Butterfly" by the rock band Heart.

chunks.title: Sue Ennis
chunks.text: She has co-written over 70 songs with Ann and Nancy Wilson of the band.

chunks.title: Sue Ennis
chunks.text: and co-wrote the theme from "The Golden Child" starring Eddie Murphy with James Bond composer, John Barry, Ann and Nancy Wilson.

chunks.title: Sue Ennis
chunks.text: Her songs have also appeared in "Thomas and the Magic Railroad", a feature film from 2000.

chunks.title: Sue Ennis
chunks.text: In 2004, she and co-writer Hummie Mann won a Soundie award (Puget Sound Advertising Award) for their jingle for State Roofing.

chunks.title: List of Heart band members
chunks.text: Heart is an American rock band that first found success in Canada and later in the United States and worldwide.

chunks.title: List of Heart band members
chunks.text: Over the group's four-decade history it has had three primary lineups, with the constant center of the group since 1974 being sisters Ann Wilson (lead singer) and Nancy Wilson (guitarist).

chunks.title: List of Heart band members
chunks.text: While it has been referred to as a duo because of the focus on leaders Ann and Nancy Wilson, Heart is a full rock group.

chunks.title: List of Heart band members
chunks.text: In its original lineup the band had six members, then five in its second incarnation, and is again at six currently.

chunks.title: The Nancy Wilson Show!
chunks.text: The Nancy Wilson Show!

chunks.title: The Nancy Wilson Show!
chunks.text: is a 1965 live album by Nancy Wilson, recorded at the Coconut Grove nightclub in Los Angeles.

chunks.title: Henry Vaccaro
chunks.text: Henry V. Vaccaro is an American businessman and author.

chunks.title: Henry Vaccaro
chunks.text: His primary business was the Henry V. Vaccaro Corporation, located in Neptune, NJ.

chunks.title: Henry Vaccaro
chunks.text: The construction company, started in 1964, built over $1 Billion in construction projects throughout New Jersey.

chunks.title: Henry Vaccaro
chunks.text: These projects included hospitals, prisons, schools, and nursing homes.

chunks.title: Henry Vaccaro
chunks.text: In 1976, he was the primary investor and owner of Kramer Guitars, also in Neptune, NJ.

chunks.title: Henry Vaccaro
chunks.text: Some endorsers of Kramer guitars included Eddie Van Halen, Bon Jovi, Mötley Crüe, Kiss (band), Heart (band), Loverboy, Skid Row (American band), Whitesnake, and Vaccaro's friend Johnny Cash, whom he met in 1972.

chunks.title: Cimar
chunks.text: Cimar was a Hoshino Gakki guitar brand.

chunks.title: Cimar
chunks.text: Designs of Cimar guitars are sometimes very similar to Hoshino Gakki's Ibanez guitar brand.

chunks.title: Cimar
chunks.text: Cimar guitars appear in Hoshino Gakki catalogues.

chunks.title: Ibanez
chunks.text: Ibanez (アイバニーズ , Aibanīzu ) is a Japanese guitar brand owned by Hoshino Gakki.

chunks.title: Ibanez
chunks.text: Based in Nagoya, Aichi, Japan, Hoshino Gakki were one of the first Japanese musical instrument companies to gain a significant foothold in import guitar sales in the United States and Europe, as well as the first brand of guitars to mass-produce the seven-string guitar and eight-string guitar.

chunks.title: Ibanez
chunks.text: Ibanez manufactures effects, accessories, amps, and instruments in Japan, China, Indonesia and in the United States (at a Los Angeles-based custom shop).

chunks.title: Ibanez
chunks.text: Currently, there are nearly 165 models of bass guitar, 130 acoustic guitars, and more than 300 electric guitars.

chunks.title: Magic Man
chunks.text: "Magic Man" is a song by the American rock band Heart.

chunks.title: Magic Man
chunks.text: The single was released in Canada in June of 1975, and in America in 1976, as the second single from the band's debut album, "Dreamboat Annie."

chunks.title: Magic Man
chunks.text: Written and composed by Ann and Nancy Wilson, the song is sung from the viewpoint of a young girl who is being seduced by an older man (referred to as a Magic Man), much to the chagrin of her mother, who calls and begs the girl to come home.

chunks.title: Magic Man
chunks.text: In an interview, Ann Wilson revealed that the "Magic Man" was her then boyfriend, band manager Michael Fisher, and that part of the song was an autobiographical tale of the beginnings of their relationship.

chunks.title: A Nancy Wilson Christmas
chunks.text: A Nancy Wilson Christmas is a 2001 studio album of Christmas music by the American singer Nancy Wilson.

chunks.title: A Nancy Wilson Christmas
chunks.text: As well as being Wilson's first album of Christmas music, it was the first album that Wilson recorded for the Manchester Craftsmen's Guild record label, MCG Jazz.

chunks.title: Nancy Wilson/Cannonball Adderley
chunks.text: Nancy Wilson/Cannonball Adderley is a 1961 studio album by Nancy Wilson with Cannonball Adderley and his quintet.

chunks.title: Nancy Wilson/Cannonball Adderley
chunks.text: Wilson considered her vocals on the album "as a sort of easy-going third horn" (Wilson quoted in the liner notes).

chunks.title: Nancy Wilson/Cannonball Adderley
chunks.text: All tracks were recorded in New York City, those with Wilson on June 27 and 29, 1961, and the instrumental tracks on August 23 and 24, 1961.

chunks.title: Heart (band)
chunks.text: Heart is an American rock band that first found success in Canada and later in the United States and worldwide.

chunks.title: Heart (band)
chunks.text: Over the group's four-decade history, it has had three primary lineups, with the constant center of the group since 1973 being sisters Ann Wilson (lead singer) and Nancy Wilson (guitarist).

chunks.title: Heart (band)
chunks.text: Heart rose to fame in the mid-1970s with music influenced by hard rock and heavy metal, as well as folk music.

chunks.title: Heart (band)
chunks.text: Their popularity declined in the early 1980s, but the band enjoyed a comeback starting in 1985 and experienced even greater success with album-oriented rock hits and hard-rock ballads into the 1990s.

chunks.title: Janine Boyd
chunks.text: Janine Boyd (born February 5, 1971) is the Representative of the 9th district of the Ohio House of Representatives.

chunks.title: Janine Boyd
chunks.text: She is the daughter of Barbara Boyd, who held the same seat from 1993 to 2000 and from 2007 to 2014.

chunks.title: Janine Boyd
chunks.text: Boyd previously served on council for Cleveland Heights, where she often faced criticism for her attendance.

chunks.title: Janine Boyd
chunks.text: In 2012, she was appointed to council to replace Phyllis Evans.

chunks.title: Janine Boyd
chunks.text: In 2014, she announced that she would seek to replace her mother, Barbara Boyd, in the Ohio House of Representatives.

chunks.title: Janine Boyd
chunks.text: She faced Republican Charles Hopson in the general election, and went on to win 85%-15%.

chunks.title: Phyllis Heineman
chunks.text: Phyllis M. Heineman (born June 28, 1948 in Mitchell, South Dakota) is an American politician and a Republican member of the South Dakota Senate representing District 13 since January 11, 2011.

chunks.title: Phyllis Heineman
chunks.text: Heineman served non-consecutively in the South Dakota Legislature from her appointment by Governor of South Dakota Bill Janklow November 2, 1999 to fill the vacancy caused by the resignation of Dana John Windhorst until January 2009 in the South Dakota House of Representatives District 13 seat.

chunks.title: Iowa House of Representatives
chunks.text: The Iowa House of Representatives is the lower house of the Iowa General Assembly.

chunks.title: Iowa House of Representatives
chunks.text: The upper house is the Iowa Senate.

chunks.title: Iowa House of Representatives
chunks.text: There are 100 seats in the Iowa House of Representatives, representing 100 single-member districts across the state, formed by dividing the 50 Senate districts in half.

chunks.title: Iowa House of Representatives
chunks.text: Each district has a population of approximately 30,464 as of the 2010 United States Census .

chunks.title: Iowa House of Representatives
chunks.text: The House of Representatives meets at the Iowa State Capitol in Des Moines.

chunks.title: Ed Case
chunks.text: Edward Espenett "Ed" Case (born September 27, 1952) is an American Democratic politician who represented Hawaii in the United States House of Representatives from 2002 to 2007.

chunks.title: Ed Case
chunks.text: Case, a Blue Dog Democrat, first came to prominence in Hawaii as majority leader of the Hawaii State Legislature and for his campaign for Governor of Hawaii in 2002.

chunks.title: Ed Case
chunks.text: First elected to the House of Representatives in 2002 in a special election to fill the seat of Patsy Mink, who died of pneumonia, Case represented Hawaii's 2nd congressional district until 2006, when he chose not to run for another term in the House of Representatives so he could challenge Senator Daniel Akaka in the Democratic primary for Akaka's U.S. Senate seat.

chunks.title: Ed Case
chunks.text: Case lost the primary election 53%–46%.

chunks.title: Emilia Sykes
chunks.text: Emilia Sykes (born January 4, 1986) is the Representative for the 34th district of the Ohio House of Representatives.

chunks.title: Emilia Sykes
chunks.text: Sykes is the daughter of former state Representatives Vernon Sykes and Barbara Sykes, who collaboratively held the same seat from 1982 to 2014, meaning that the seat has been represented by a member of the Sykes family for over thirty years.

chunks.title: Emilia Sykes
chunks.text: Sykes is a graduate of Kent State University and received both a JD and a Master of Public Health from the University of Florida.

chunks.title: Emilia Sykes
chunks.text: She also has served as an administrative adviser in the Summit County fiscal office.

chunks.title: Emilia Sykes
chunks.text: In 2013, Sykes decided to run for the Ohio House of Representatives to succeed her father, Vernon Sykes, who was term-limited.

chunks.title: Emilia Sykes
chunks.text: She defeated Summit County Councilman Frank Communale to take the Democratic nomination.

chunks.title: Emilia Sykes
chunks.text: Sykes defeated Republican Cynthia Blake 72%-28% to take the seat.

chunks.title: Washington House of Representatives
chunks.text: The Washington House of Representatives is the lower house of the Washington State Legislature, and along with the Washington State Senate makes up the legislature of the US state of Washington.

chunks.title: Washington House of Representatives
chunks.text: It is composed of 98 Representatives from 49 districts, each of which elects one Senator and two members of the House.

chunks.title: Washington House of Representatives
chunks.text: All members of the House are elected to a two-year term without term limits.

chunks.title: Washington House of Representatives
chunks.text: The House meets at the Legislative Building in Olympia.

chunks.title: Franklin Coslett
chunks.text: Franklin Coslett (October 20, 1921 – January 28, 2011) is a former Republican member of the Pennsylvania House of Representatives who served as the State Representative for the 120th legislative district of Pennsylvania from 1979 to 1986.

chunks.title: Franklin Coslett
chunks.text: His tenure in Harrisburg was an era marked by superb constituent service, especially in aiding seniors in receiving prescription drug benefits.

chunks.title: Franklin Coslett
chunks.text: Before his time in the State House, Coslett was a civic leader in his hometown of Kingston, Pennsylvania, the largest municipality in and the seat of the 120th district.

chunks.title: Franklin Coslett
chunks.text: Indeed, at one point, he served as the President of the Kingston borough council.

chunks.title: Franklin Coslett
chunks.text: After retiring from the Pennsylvania House in 1986, Coslett was succeeded by Republican Scott Dietterick.

chunks.title: Franklin Coslett
chunks.text: The seat Coslett and Dietterick occupied is currently held by Republican Aaron Kaufer, who succeeded longtime Democratic representative Phyllis Mundy after Mundy's 2014 retirement.

chunks.title: Minnesota House of Representatives
chunks.text: The Minnesota House of Representatives is the lower house of the Legislature of the U.S. state of Minnesota.

chunks.title: Minnesota House of Representatives
chunks.text: There are 134 members, twice as many as the Minnesota Senate.

chunks.title: Minnesota House of Representatives
chunks.text: Floor sessions are held in the north wing of the State Capitol in Saint Paul.

chunks.title: Phyllis Kahn
chunks.text: Phyllis Lorberblatt Kahn (born March 23, 1937) is a Minnesota politician and former member of the Minnesota House of Representatives.

chunks.title: Phyllis Kahn
chunks.text: A member of the Minnesota Democratic–Farmer–Labor Party (DFL), she represented District 60B, which included portions of the city of Minneapolis in Hennepin County in the Twin Cities metropolitan area.

chunks.title: Hideo Hiraoka
chunks.text: Hideo Hiraoka (平岡 秀夫 , Hiraoka Hideo , born January 14, 1954) is a Japanese politician of the Democratic Party of Japan, a member of the House of Representatives in the Diet (national legislature).

chunks.title: Hideo Hiraoka
chunks.text: A native of Iwakuni, Yamaguchi, Hiraoka passed the bar exam and civil service exam prior to his graduation at the University of Tokyo.

chunks.title: Hideo Hiraoka
chunks.text: In 1976 he entered the Ministry of Finance which he joined before resigning in 1998 after working in the National Tax Agency's corporate tax department.

chunks.title: Hideo Hiraoka
chunks.text: In 2000, after leaving the ministry, he was elected to a seat of the House of Representatives for the first time; the district he represented, Yamaguchi Prefecture's No. 2 district, was previously a stronghold for the rival Liberal Democratic Party.

chunks.title: Hideo Hiraoka
chunks.text: Following a large-scale upturn by the Liberal Democratic Party, Hiraoka lost his seat by 588 votes, remaining in the Lower House through a process known as proportional representation.

chunks.title: Hideo Hiraoka
chunks.text: In 2008 he took back the Yamaguchi No. 2 seat, marking his fifth term as its representative for the Lower House.

chunks.title: Hideo Hiraoka
chunks.text: Hiraoka was later appointed state secretary for internal affairs and communications in 2010.

chunks.title: Hideo Hiraoka
chunks.text: In September 2011 he was appointed Minister of Justice in the cabinet of newly appointed prime minister Yoshihiko Noda.

chunks.title: Religion in Ghana
chunks.text: Christianity is the largest religion in Ghana, with approximately 71.2% of the country's population being members of various Christian denominations as of 2010 census.

chunks.title: Religion in Ghana
chunks.text: The religious composition of Ghana in the first postindependence population census of 1960 was 25 percent Muslim, 23 percent traditionalist, 41 percent Christian, and the rest (about 9 percent) other.

chunks.title: Religion in Ghana
chunks.text: A breakdown of the 1960 population according to Christian sects showed that 25 percent were Protestant (non-Pentecostal); 13 percent, Roman Catholic; 2 percent, Protestant (Pentecostal); and 1 percent, Independent African Churches.

chunks.title: Religion in Ghana
chunks.text: The 1970 population census did not present figures on the religious composition of the nation.

chunks.title: National Archives of Zambia
chunks.text: The National Archives of Zambia preserves the archives of the Republic of Zambia and maintains its legal deposit library.

chunks.title: National Archives of Zambia
chunks.text: The library holds 70,000 volumes.

chunks.title: National Archives of Zambia
chunks.text: Its headquarters is located in Ridgeway in the city of Lusaka.

chunks.title: Gaboš
chunks.text: Gaboš (Serbian Cyrillic: ) is a village in Vukovar-Srijem County, Croatia.

chunks.title: Gaboš
chunks.text: There are 613 inhabitants, the majority of the population which are Serbs, who make up 95% of the population according to the 2001 population census.

chunks.title: National Archives of Namibia
chunks.text: The National Archives of Namibia is the national archives of Namibia, located in Windhoek and it was established in 1939.

chunks.title: National Archives of Namibia
chunks.text: It holds 5600 maps, 61000 photographs, 2000 audio cassettes, 450 films and a complete collection of all local newspapers from 1897 to 1962.

chunks.title: National Archives of Namibia
chunks.text: It shares a building with the National Library of Namibia.

chunks.title: National Archives of Bangladesh
chunks.text: The National Archives of Bangladesh (NAB) are based in Dhaka and contain 225,000 volumes of documents in addition to books, microfilm rolls and newspaper clippings.

chunks.title: National Archives of Bangladesh
chunks.text: The archives were founded in 1973 by the government of Bangladesh and are administered by the Directorate of National Archives and Libraries.

chunks.title: National Archives of Bangladesh
chunks.text: Located in a rented building near the campus of Dhaka University until 1985, the collections are now housed in a purpose-built part of the National Library of Bangladesh complex in Sher-e-Bangla Nagar.

chunks.title: National Archives and Library of Ethiopia
chunks.text: The National Archives and Library of Ethiopia, located in Addis Ababa, is the national library and archives of the country.

chunks.title: National Archives and Library of Ethiopia
chunks.text: The library was inaugurated in 1944 by Emperor Haile Selassie and began service with books donated by the emperor.

chunks.title: National Archives of Mauritania
chunks.text: The Archives Nationales de Mauritanie (National Archives of Mauritania) is the national archives of Mauritania.

chunks.title: National Archives of Mauritania
chunks.text: It was founded in 1955 and hold 3,000 volumes.

chunks.title: National Archives of Mauritania
chunks.text: As of 2007 it was located on Avenue de l'Indépendance.

chunks.title: National Archives of Mauritania
chunks.text: Directors have included Mohamed Ould Gaouad (circa 1974), Izidh Bih Ould Sidi Mohamed (circa 2007), and Mohamed Moctar Ould Sidi Mohamed (circa 2017).

chunks.title: List of ethnic groups in Ethiopia
chunks.text: This is a list of ethnic groups in Ethiopia that are officially recognized by the government.

chunks.title: List of ethnic groups in Ethiopia
chunks.text: It is a list taken from the 2007 Ethiopian National Census: Population size and percentage of Ethiopia's total population according to the 1994 and 2007 censuses follows each entry.

chunks.title: Bibliothèque et Archives nationales du Québec
chunks.text: Bibliothèque et Archives nationales du Québec (BAnQ, unofficially translated as National Library and Archives of Québec) is a Québec governmental organization who manages the legal deposit and national archives systems of the province as well as its national library, which is located in the Grande Bibliothèque in Montreal.

chunks.title: Bibliothèque et Archives nationales du Québec
chunks.text: It is born out of a merger between the Bibliothèque nationale du Québec (BNQ) and the Archives nationales du Québec, in 2006.

chunks.title: Bibliothèque et Archives nationales du Québec
chunks.text: The Bibliothèque nationale du Québec had previously merged with the Grande bibliothèque du Québec in 2002.

chunks.title: Addis Ababa
chunks.text: Addis Ababa (Amharic: አዲስ አበባ "Addis Abäba " ] , "new flower"; Oromo: "Finfinne" , ] "Natural Spring(s)") or Addis Abeba (the spelling used by the official Ethiopian Mapping Authority), is the capital and largest city of Ethiopia.

chunks.title: Addis Ababa
chunks.text: It has a population of 3,384,569 according to the 2007 population census, with annual growth rate of 3.8%.

chunks.title: Addis Ababa
chunks.text: This number has been increased from the originally published 2,738,248 figure and appears to be still largely underestimated.

chunks.title: Richmond Valley Council
chunks.text: Richmond Valley Council (RVC) is a local government area on the Northern Rivers region of north-eastern New South Wales, Australia.

chunks.title: Richmond Valley Council
chunks.text: RVC services an area of 3051 km2 and draws its name from the Richmond River, which flows through most of the council area.

chunks.title: Richmond Valley Council
chunks.text: The area under management is located adjacent to the Bruxner Highway, Pacific Highway, and the North Coast railway line.

chunks.title: Wollongbar, New South Wales
chunks.text: Wollongbar is a town (2011 population: 2,396) in the Northern Rivers region of New South Wales, Australia.

chunks.title: Wollongbar, New South Wales
chunks.text: The town is located on the Bruxner Highway between the towns of Lismore and Alstonville.

chunks.title: Casino, New South Wales
chunks.text: Casino is a town in the Northern Rivers area of New South Wales, Australia, with a population of 9,629 people at the 2011 census .

chunks.title: Casino, New South Wales
chunks.text: It lies on the banks of the Richmond River and is situated at the junction of the Bruxner Highway and the Summerland Way.

chunks.title: Tabulam
chunks.text: Tabulam is a rural village in the far north-east of New South Wales, Australia, 800 kilometres from the state capital, Sydney.

chunks.title: Tabulam
chunks.text: Tabulam is located on the Bruxner Highway (Highway 44) between Tenterfield and Casino and on the Clarence River.

chunks.title: Tabulam
chunks.text: According to the 2006 Census, there were 573 people living in Tabulam.

chunks.title: Tabulam
chunks.text: Tabulam is locally administered by Kyogle Council.

chunks.title: Mummulgum
chunks.text: Mummulgum is a small rural village in the Northern Rivers region of New South Wales, Australia, 740 kilometres from the state capital, Sydney.

chunks.title: Mummulgum
chunks.text: Mummulgum is located on Shannon Brook between Tenterfield and Casino on the Bruxner Highway (Highway 44).

chunks.title: Mummulgum

chunks.title: Tom Courtenay
chunks.text: Sir Thomas Daniel Courtenay ( ; born 25 February 1937) is an English actor who came to prominence in the early 1960s with a succession of films, including "The Loneliness of the Long Distance Runner" (1962), "Billy Liar" (1963), and "Doctor Zhivago" (1965).
